lessons.title: The Skeletal System
lessons.summary: The skeleton is not a passive frame: it supports, protects, moves, forms blood cells and stores minerals and fat.

knowledge.title: Five jobs of the skeleton
knowledge.text:
The skeleton is not a passive frame: it supports, protects, moves, forms blood cells and stores minerals and fat.

Bones create a firm framework that supports softer tissues and shields organs such as the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs. At joints, bones also act as levers. Skeletal muscles pull on those levers to create movement and help expand the thorax during breathing.

Red marrow forms blood cells through hematopoiesis. Bone also stores calcium and phosphorus, while yellow marrow stores fat. These roles explain why skeletal health is linked to movement, circulation and mineral homeostasis rather than being an isolated topic.

Support and protection are structural roles.

Bones and muscles work as lever-and-force partners.

Red marrow forms blood cells.

Bone is a regulated mineral reservoir.

Support · Protect · Levers · Marrow · Bank

Think of bone as the body’s support-and-storage bank.

The mineral matrix makes bone hard, but living cells, vessels and nerves make it dynamic.

A nutrition professional can explain why bone health involves adequate substrate and whole-body regulation, while diagnosis and treatment remain clinical responsibilities.

Framework: Supports tissues and posture

Shield: Protects vital organs

Lever: Transmits muscular force

Marrow: Forms blood cells or stores fat

Reservoir: Stores calcium and phosphorus
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Build, maintain, resorb
knowledge.text:
Osteoblasts deposit bone, osteocytes maintain it, and osteoclasts resorb it during remodeling.

Bone formation begins with osteoblasts. As the surrounding matrix matures, many become osteocytes housed in small spaces called lacunae. Osteoclasts remove bone, which is essential for shaping, repair and mineral regulation rather than simply being destructive.

Intramembranous ossification builds bone within connective membranes, especially in the skull. Endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage model and forms most other bones. Remodeling continues after growth has ended and responds to mechanical load and hormonal signals.

Osteoblast = deposition.

Osteocyte = mature maintenance cell.

Osteoclast = resorption.

Intramembranous and endochondral ossification start from different templates.

Builders · Lodgers · Clean-up

Blasts build, cytes live in the matrix, clasts clear bone.

Parathyroid hormone and calcitonin participate in blood-calcium regulation; bone is one part of that larger system.

Calcium and vitamin D matter to bone biology, but a dietary history alone cannot determine bone density or fracture risk.

Deposit: Osteoblast lays matrix

Maintain: Osteocyte monitors local tissue

Resorb: Osteoclast removes matrix

Renew: New matrix replaces remodeled area
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Compact and spongy bone
knowledge.text:
Compact bone is organized into osteons; spongy bone forms trabeculae around marrow spaces.

An osteon is the repeating structural unit of compact bone. A central canal carries vessels, concentric lamellae form rings, osteocytes occupy lacunae, and canaliculi create tiny communication routes through the hard matrix.

Spongy or cancellous bone is arranged as a lattice of trabeculae. Its spaces contain marrow, and its architecture places material along lines of stress without making the bone solid throughout. Compact and spongy tissue therefore solve different mechanical problems.

Central canal carries vessels.

Lamellae are concentric layers.

Lacunae house osteocytes.

Canaliculi connect spaces.

Trabeculae form the spongy lattice.

Canal · Lamellae · Lacunae · Canaliculi

Walk outward from an osteon’s center.

Bone looks solid macroscopically, yet microscopic channels keep living cells supplied.

Red-marrow distribution changes with age, which is why “bone marrow” is not a single uniform tissue throughout the skeleton.

Central canal: Vessels and nerves

Lamellae: Concentric matrix rings

Lacunae: Osteocyte spaces

Canaliculi: Microscopic connecting channels
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Long bones and shape classes
knowledge.text:
A long bone has a shaft, ends, coverings and a marrow cavity; “long” describes shape, not absolute size.

The diaphysis is the shaft of a long bone, the epiphyses are its ends, and the metaphyses are transition regions. Periosteum covers the outer surface except at articular cartilage, while endosteum lines internal surfaces. The medullary cavity occupies the shaft.

Bones are also classified as long, short, flat, irregular or sesamoid. Flat bones provide broad protection or muscle attachment; irregular bones have complex shapes; sesamoid bones develop within tendons. Classification helps predict form and function.

Diaphysis = shaft.

Epiphysis = end.

Periosteum is external; endosteum is internal.

Patella is a sesamoid bone.

Diaphysis = Drive shaft; Metaphysis = Middle transition; Epiphysis = End

Use position to retrieve each name.

The femur is long, but tiny phalanges are also classified as long bones because of their proportions.

Mechanical loading is one influence on remodeling; it should not be reduced to a promise that one food or exercise prevents every bone problem.

Epiphysis: Expanded end

Metaphysis: Transition/growth region

Diaphysis: Shaft and medullary cavity

Periosteum: Fibrovascular outer covering
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Cranium, face and openings
knowledge.text:
Cranial bones protect the brain; facial bones shape the face and support the air and food passages.

The axial skeleton begins with the skull. Cranial bones include the frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid bones. The sphenoid spans the cranial floor and helps bind several cranial bones together. Facial bones include the maxillae, zygomatic bones and mandible.

Openings and processes reveal function. The foramen magnum in the occipital bone transmits the spinal cord, while condyles articulate with the first cervical vertebra. Sutures are fibrous joints that unite skull bones.

Cranial and facial bones have different organizing roles.

Mandible forms the lower jaw.

Sphenoid anchors across the cranial floor.

Foramen magnum connects cranial and vertebral spaces.

Frontal · Occipital · Sphenoid · Temporal · Ethmoid · Parietal

A compact cue for the main cranial-bone set.

The hyoid is part of the axial skeleton but does not articulate directly with another bone.

Knowing skull landmarks helps a learner interpret terms in swallowing, dental and neurological discussions without diagnosing injury.

Frontal: Forehead and anterior cranial roof

Occipital: Posterior skull and foramen magnum

Sphenoid: Central cranial-floor anchor

Mandible: Movable lower jaw
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Vertebral column and thorax
knowledge.text:
The vertebral column protects the spinal cord; ribs and sternum protect thoracic organs and support breathing.

The vertebral column is organized into cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccygeal regions. The atlas supports the skull and the axis permits rotation. Normal curves distribute load; exaggerated or lateral curves are described with specific terms such as kyphosis, lordosis and scoliosis.

The thoracic cage includes thoracic vertebrae, ribs and sternum. True ribs attach directly to the sternum through costal cartilage, false ribs attach indirectly, and floating ribs lack anterior attachment. The sternum includes the manubrium, body and xiphoid process.

Seven cervical, twelve thoracic and five lumbar vertebrae precede the fused regions.

Atlas and axis have specialized roles.

True ribs attach directly; floating ribs do not attach anteriorly.

The sternum is the breastbone.

7 · 12 · 5

Seven cervical, twelve thoracic and five lumbar—breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5.

“True” and “false” describe rib attachment patterns, not whether a rib is complete or functional.

Posture and curvature terms describe anatomy; persistent pain or suspected injury requires appropriate clinical assessment.

Cervical: Neck; C1–C7

Thoracic: Rib-bearing; T1–T12

Lumbar: Lower back; L1–L5

Sacrum/coccyx: Fused terminal regions

knowledge.title: Girdles and limbs
knowledge.text:
The pectoral and pelvic girdles attach the upper and lower limbs to the axial skeleton.

The pectoral girdle consists of clavicles and scapulae. It prioritizes mobility, giving the upper limb a wide range of movement. The upper limb continues through humerus, radius and ulna to carpals, metacarpals and phalanges.

The pelvic girdle forms a stronger weight-bearing ring. Each hip bone is formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis; the acetabulum receives the femoral head. The lower limb continues through femur, patella, tibia and fibula to tarsals, metatarsals and phalanges.

Pectoral girdle favors mobility.

Pelvic girdle favors stability and weight transfer.

Radius/ulna are forearm bones.

Tibia/fibula are leg bones.

Carpals are wrist; tarsals are ankle/foot.

Carpals = hands; tarsals = feet

A car is handled with the hands; tar is under the feet.

The patella is the largest sesamoid bone and develops within the quadriceps tendon.

Bone names support accurate movement and injury communication but do not replace assessment of pain, swelling or function.

Upper limb: Scapula → humerus → radius/ulna → carpals

Lower limb: Hip → femur → tibia/fibula → tarsals

knowledge.title: Bone health is a system question
knowledge.text:
Bone strength reflects matrix, cells, hormones, nutrients, load and time—not one nutrient in isolation.

Calcium and phosphorus contribute to mineralized matrix, while vitamin D supports calcium absorption. Protein supplies matrix components. Hormones help regulate deposition and release, and mechanical load influences remodeling. Adequacy across these factors matters more than a single “bone food.”

Disorders illustrate different mechanisms: rickets and osteomalacia involve impaired mineralization, osteoporosis involves reduced bone mass and altered structure, and Paget disease involves disordered remodeling. A fracture is a break in bone or associated cartilage and requires clinical care.

Mineralization and remodeling are different processes.

Vitamin D supports calcium handling.

Osteoporosis is not simply “low calcium.”

Fracture, rickets and Paget disease describe different problems.

Matrix · Inputs · load · endocrine signals · time

Bone health emerges from interacting influences.

An adult can have adequate current intake yet still require assessment for bone-density or fracture concerns.

Nutrition counselling can support adequate intake and feasible habits, while risk evaluation, diagnosis and treatment belong with qualified clinicians.

Matrix: Collagen-rich framework plus mineral

Cells: Deposit, maintain and resorb

Signals: Hormonal regulation

Inputs: Nutrients and mechanical load

Time: Growth, aging and repair

lessons.title: The Articular System
lessons.summary: Structure and movement are two different naming systems.

knowledge.title: Structural and functional classifications
knowledge.text:
Structure and movement are two different naming systems.

A joint, or articulation, is where two or more skeletal elements meet. Structural classification asks what material joins the bones: fibrous tissue, cartilage, or a fluid-filled synovial cavity.

Functional classification asks how much movement is possible. A synarthrosis is essentially immovable, an amphiarthrosis allows limited movement, and a diarthrosis moves freely. Most limb joints are diarthroses and structurally synovial.

Fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial are structural groups.

Synarthroses do not move.

Amphiarthroses move slightly.

Diarthroses move freely.

Synarthrosis · Amphiarthrosis · Diarthrosis

Think still, a little, dynamic.

The two systems overlap, but their terms are not interchangeable.

Precise movement language helps a nutrition professional document mobility barriers without labeling their cause.

Structure: What physically joins the bones?

Function: How much movement occurs?

Key pairing: Synovial joints are usually diarthroses
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Fibrous and cartilaginous joints
knowledge.text:
Less motion generally brings more stability.

Fibrous joints are united by dense connective tissue. Skull sutures are nearly immovable; a syndesmosis uses a ligament or membrane between bones; a gomphosis anchors a tooth in its socket.

Cartilaginous joints join bones with cartilage. A synchondrosis uses hyaline cartilage, as in an epiphyseal plate before it closes. A symphysis uses fibrocartilage and allows limited movement, as at the pubic symphysis or between vertebral bodies.

Suture and gomphosis are fibrous.

Syndesmosis uses fibrous tissue.

Synchondrosis uses hyaline cartilage.

Symphysis uses fibrocartilage.

SynCHondrosis uses hyaline Cartilage

The shared sound helps separate it from a symphysis.

The former growth plate between a diaphysis and epiphysis is a classic synchondrosis.

Joint structure can explain why a movement limitation is mechanically plausible, but it does not establish a diagnosis.

Suture: Interlocking skull bones

Gomphosis: Tooth in socket

Synchondrosis: Hyaline cartilage bridge

Symphysis: Fibrocartilage pad
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Inside a synovial joint
knowledge.text:
Articular cartilage reduces friction; fluid lubricates; ligaments guide and restrain.

At a synovial joint, the bone ends are capped by smooth articular cartilage and separated by a cavity. A capsule encloses the joint; its fibrous outer layer stabilizes while its inner synovial membrane produces synovial fluid.

Ligaments connect bone to bone. Bursae are small fluid-filled sacs positioned where skin, tendon, ligament, or bone might rub. Menisci or discs in some joints improve fit and distribute load.

Articular cartilage covers opposing bone ends.

Synovial fluid lubricates and nourishes cartilage.

Ligaments connect bone to bone.

Bursae reduce friction at pressure points.

Cartilage · Capsule · Fluid · Ligament · Bursa

Rebuild the joint from the surfaces outward.

Subcutaneous bursae lie between skin and a bony prominence, such as around the knee or elbow.

When a client reports pain or swelling, adapt movement-based goals and refer rather than trying to identify the injured structure.

Cartilage: Smooth bearing surface

Cavity + fluid: Low-friction space

Capsule: Enclosure and stability

Ligament: Bone-to-bone restraint

Bursa: Friction-reducing sac
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Six joint shapes
knowledge.text:
Shape predicts available axes of motion.

Plane joints glide; hinge joints mainly flex and extend; pivot joints rotate around one axis. Condyloid joints move in two planes, saddle joints allow broad biaxial movement, and ball-and-socket joints move around multiple axes.

Use anchor examples: intercarpal plane, elbow hinge, proximal radioulnar pivot, knuckle condyloid, thumb saddle, and shoulder or hip ball-and-socket. Ball-and-socket mobility is broad, but stability still depends on socket depth, capsule, ligaments and muscles.

Hinge and pivot are uniaxial.

Condyloid and saddle are biaxial.

Ball-and-socket is multiaxial.

The thumb carpometacarpal joint is saddle shaped.

Plane · Hinge · Pivot · Condyloid · Saddle · Ball-and-socket

Use the first letters to recall the six shapes.

The hip and shoulder share a joint type but differ in stability because their surrounding anatomy differs.

Knowing axes of motion can help modify exercises around a known limitation while staying within an assigned care plan.

Plane: Glide

Hinge: Door-like arc

Pivot: Axial rotation

Condyloid: Two-plane oval

Saddle: Two-plane reciprocal curves

Ball-and-socket: Multiaxial sphere
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Angle and midline movements
knowledge.text:
Flex/extend change an angle; abduct/adduct change distance from the midline.

Flexion decreases the angle between bones, while extension increases it. Hyperextension continues beyond the anatomical position. Abduction moves a part away from the midline; adduction returns it toward the midline.

Circumduction combines flexion, extension, abduction and adduction so the distal end traces a circle. Rotation turns a bone around its long axis.

Flexion decreases an angle.

Extension increases an angle.

Abduction moves away from the midline.

Adduction moves toward the midline.

ABduction begins with the same sound as away

Then adduction means add it back.

Pronation is not movement of the jaw; in the forearm it turns the palm posteriorly/downward from anatomical position.

Use neutral descriptions such as “difficulty with ankle dorsiflexion” rather than assuming the cause.

Flexion: Close the angle

Extension: Open the angle

Abduction: Away from midline

Adduction: Add toward midline

Rotation: Turn around an axis
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Special movements
knowledge.text:
Feet, forearms, jaw and shoulder girdles use specialized vocabulary.

Dorsiflexion brings the top of the foot toward the shin; plantar flexion points the foot. Inversion turns the sole inward and eversion turns it outward. Pronation and supination describe forearm rotation.

Elevation raises a body part and depression lowers it. Protraction moves a structure anteriorly, while retraction moves it posteriorly. Opposition brings the thumb across the palm to meet a fingertip.

Dorsiflexion lifts the foot.

Inversion and eversion apply to the foot.

Elevation and depression are opposites.

Opposition is central to thumb function.

Supination holds a bowl of soup

Palm-up imagery separates it from pronation.

Movement descriptions assume the anatomical position unless the context says otherwise.

Movement vocabulary can make accessibility planning specific: reach, grip, gait and meal preparation each demand different motions.

Dorsi / plantar: Foot up / point

Inversion / eversion: Sole in / out

Pronation / supination: Palm down / up

Elevation / depression: Raise / lower

Protraction / retraction: Forward / back

knowledge.title: Sprain, strain and dislocation
knowledge.text:
The words identify different structures and events.

A sprain injures a ligament; a strain injures muscle or tendon. A dislocation occurs when articulating bone surfaces are displaced, while subluxation is partial displacement. These require appropriate clinical assessment rather than self-classification.

Repetitive loading can irritate tendons or bursae and may contribute to compression syndromes such as carpal tunnel syndrome. A laminectomy is a surgical removal of part of a vertebral lamina to create space; it is not simply another word for dislocation.

Sprain involves a ligament.

Strain involves muscle or tendon.

Dislocation changes joint congruence.

Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa.

SPrain pairs with supporting ligament

Contrast it with STRain of muscle/tendon.

A temporarily displaced joint is still a safety concern even if it seems to move back into place.

Nutrition support may help a person meet general recovery needs, but it does not replace assessment or rehabilitation.

Ligament: Sprain

Muscle/tendon: Strain

Joint alignment: Dislocation

Bursa: Bursitis

Joint overall: Arthritis
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Arthritis patterns without shortcuts
knowledge.text:
Arthritis is a broad category; several mechanisms can affect a joint.

Osteoarthritis involves degeneration of joint structures over time and load. Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune connective-tissue disorder that often inflames small joints. Gout follows deposition of urate crystals, commonly affecting the joint at the base of the large toe.

Shared symptoms such as pain, stiffness or swelling do not make the conditions equivalent. History, examination and testing guide diagnosis; anatomy study should help you understand the involved structures, not diagnose from a symptom list.

Arthritis means joint inflammation/disease as a broad label.

Osteoarthritis is degenerative.

Rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune/systemic.

Gout involves urate crystals.

Osteoarthritis · Rheumatoid · Gout

Name the mechanism after the label.

Gout can involve other joints even though the first metatarsophalangeal joint is a classic site.

Nutrition professionals can support evidence-based dietary goals within scope while coordinating with medical management.

Wear/degeneration: Osteoarthritis

Autoimmune inflammation: Rheumatoid arthritis

Crystal deposition: Gout

lessons.title: The Muscular System
lessons.summary: Control, striation, cell shape and location separate the three types.

knowledge.title: Three muscle tissues
knowledge.text:
Control, striation, cell shape and location separate the three types.

Skeletal muscle is striated, usually voluntary, and moves the skeleton. Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary and forms the heart wall. Smooth muscle lacks visible striations, is involuntary, and moves material through hollow organs and blood vessels.

All three convert chemical energy into force, yet their cell organization and control differ. Cardiac activity is influenced by the autonomic nervous system; this does not make cardiac tissue smooth muscle.

Skeletal: striated and voluntary.

Cardiac: striated and involuntary.

Smooth: nonstriated and involuntary.

Cardiac and smooth activity are autonomically influenced.

Skeletal · Cardiac · Smooth

Move from body wall to heart to hollow organs.

A tissue can be striated without being voluntarily controlled.

Avoid promising that a food or supplement can selectively change one muscle type.

Skeletal: Bones; voluntary

Cardiac: Heart; involuntary

Smooth: Hollow organs; involuntary

knowledge.title: The nested organization
knowledge.text:
Connective-tissue layers package force-producing cells.

Epimysium surrounds the whole muscle. Perimysium surrounds a fascicle, and endomysium surrounds each muscle fiber. A fiber contains many myofibrils, which are repeating chains of sarcomeres.

Within each sarcomere, thin actin and thick myosin filaments form the banding pattern. The light I band contains thin filaments; the dark A band spans thick filaments. Tendons transmit the combined pull to bone.

Epimysium: whole muscle.

Perimysium: fascicle.

Endomysium: fiber.

Myofibrils contain repeating sarcomeres.

Actin is thin; myosin is thick.

Epimysium · Perimysium · Endomysium

Move from the entire muscle to packets to each fiber.

A fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibers, not one fiber or one myofibril.

Adequate dietary protein supports whole-body protein turnover; it does not bypass training, recovery or clinical factors.

Muscle: Epimysium

Fascicle: Perimysium

Fiber: Endomysium

Myofibril: Sarcomere chain

Sarcomere: Actin + myosin

knowledge.title: Neuromuscular activation
knowledge.text:
Acetylcholine starts a muscle-fiber action potential.

When a motor-neuron impulse reaches the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine is released. It binds receptors on the sarcolemma, changing ion permeability; sodium entry helps depolarize the membrane and launch an action potential.

The signal travels along the sarcolemma and down T tubules. This triggers the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium around the myofibrils. The electrical message has now become a chemical permission signal for contraction.

Acetylcholine is the neuromuscular transmitter.

Sodium is concentrated outside the resting fiber.

The action potential enters T tubules.

The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium.

Acetylcholine · T tubule · Calcium

Recall the activation sequence.

Calcium release here is intracellular signaling, not a claim that an acute calcium supplement directly causes a stronger contraction.

Explain nutrient roles as background physiology while keeping performance and symptom claims evidence based.

Motor neuron: Impulse arrives

ACh: Crosses junction

Sarcolemma/T tubule: Conducts signal

SR: Releases Ca²⁺
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Sliding filaments and ATP
knowledge.text:
Filaments slide past one another; they do not become shorter.

Calcium binds the regulatory system associated with troponin and tropomyosin, exposing binding sites on actin. Energized myosin heads attach, pivot, and pull thin filaments toward the sarcomere center.

ATP binding releases myosin from actin; ATP breakdown re-cocks the head for another cycle. As cycling repeats, Z lines approach, the I band and H zone narrow, and the A band stays the same length.

Calcium exposes binding sites.

Myosin forms cross-bridges with actin.

ATP is needed for detachment and re-energizing.

The A band remains constant.

Calcium · Attach · Pull · Release · Reset

Use the cycle rather than memorizing isolated steps.

Rigor after death reflects loss of ATP-dependent cross-bridge release, illustrating ATP’s role in relaxation.

Energy availability matters to muscle physiology, but fatigue has multiple neural, metabolic and environmental contributors.

Expose: Calcium shifts regulators

Attach: Myosin binds actin

Pull: Power stroke

Release: ATP binds

Reset: ATP is hydrolyzed
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Three routes to ATP
knowledge.text:
Stored ATP is small; phosphocreatine, glycolysis and aerobic metabolism replenish it.

Muscle stores only a brief supply of ATP. Phosphocreatine rapidly transfers a phosphate to ADP and is especially useful during short, intense work. Anaerobic glycolysis produces ATP quickly from glucose but yields lactate when pyruvate cannot be processed aerobically at the same rate.

Aerobic metabolism in mitochondria uses oxygen and fuel molecules to generate much more ATP, supporting longer-duration activity. All systems overlap; their relative contribution shifts with intensity, duration, training and recovery.

Phosphocreatine rapidly buffers ATP.

Glycolysis can proceed without oxygen.

Aerobic metabolism yields more ATP over time.

Lactate is associated with anaerobic processing in this text’s framework.

Phosphocreatine · Glycolysis · Aerobic

Order the major replenishment routes from rapid to sustained.

Phosphocreatine is the phosphorylated molecule named in the source quiz, whereas creatine alone is not the immediate phosphate donor.

Meal timing and adequacy can support training, but individualized sport recommendations depend on context and scope.

Stored ATP: Seconds

Phosphocreatine: Rapid high power

Anaerobic glycolysis: Fast, limited yield

Aerobic metabolism: Slower, sustained yield
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Tone and contraction types
knowledge.text:
Length change and tension are separate features.

Muscle tone is a low level of ongoing activation that helps posture and readiness. In an isotonic contraction, tension moves a load and muscle length changes: concentric action shortens; eccentric action lengthens under tension.

In an isometric contraction, tension rises but overall muscle length and the joint angle remain relatively constant. Repeated overload can promote hypertrophy; disuse can lead to atrophy.

Tone supports posture.

Concentric shortens under load.

Eccentric lengthens under load.

Isometric creates tension without visible shortening.

Disuse promotes atrophy.

IsoMETRIC keeps the measurement similar

Isotonic involves movement in the simplified textbook contrast.

Holding a weight still is isometric; lifting it is typically concentric, not isometric.

When appetite or access limits intake during rehabilitation, coordinate nutrition support with the care team rather than prescribing exercise.

Concentric: Shorten

Eccentric: Lengthen under load

Isometric: Hold length

Tone: Baseline activation

knowledge.title: Origin, insertion and teamwork
knowledge.text:
Movement emerges from groups, not one muscle acting alone.

The origin is usually the less movable attachment; the insertion is usually the more movable attachment where the effect is seen. During an action, the prime mover or agonist supplies the main force, an antagonist opposes or controls it, and synergists assist or stabilize.

Muscle names can encode clues: rectus means straight, oblique signals diagonal fibers, maximus indicates large size, and terms such as flexor, adductor or levator describe action.

Insertion is typically the movable attachment.

Agonist is the prime mover.

Antagonist opposes or controls.

Synergists assist.

Names often predict action or anatomy.

Agonist acts · antagonist inhibits/controls · synergist supports

Use roles rather than memorizing pairs.

The same muscle may be an agonist in one movement and an antagonist in another.

Functional language can identify tasks a client finds difficult without assuming weakness, injury or motivation.

Agonist: Main action

Antagonist: Opposes/controls

Synergist: Assists

Origin: Less movable

Insertion: More movable

knowledge.title: Anchor muscles by function
knowledge.text:
Connect a familiar action to each name.

Frontalis raises the eyebrows; rectus abdominis flexes the trunk; the superior rectus elevates the eye. Flexor digitorum longus flexes the toes, while tibialis anterior contributes to dorsiflexion.

Action words generalize: abductors move away from the midline, adductors return toward it, levators raise, depressors lower, flexors decrease an angle and extensors increase it. Learn the rule first, then the regional example.

Frontalis raises eyebrows.

Rectus abdominis flexes trunk.

Flexor digitorum longus flexes toes.

Superior rectus raises the eye.

Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes.

Region + direction + action

Decode the components before rote recall.

Dorsiflexion appears in both the joint and muscle lessons because movement vocabulary bridges systems.

Use task substitutions and accessible food preparation when movement is limited, in coordination with clinical recommendations.

Frontalis: Forehead/eyebrows

Rectus abdominis: Trunk flexion

Flexor digitorum longus: Toe flexion

Superior rectus: Eye elevation

Tibialis anterior: Dorsiflexion

lessons.title: The Nervous System: Introduction, Spinal Cord, and Spinal Nerves
lessons.summary: Location and direction create the master map.

knowledge.title: CNS, PNS, sensory and motor
knowledge.text:
Location and direction create the master map.

The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) includes nerves and ganglia outside the CNS. Together they form a rapid control and communication network.

Sensory, or afferent, neurons carry information toward the CNS. Motor, or efferent, neurons carry commands from the CNS to muscles and glands. Interneurons inside the CNS connect and process these pathways.

CNS = brain + spinal cord.

PNS = nerves + ganglia.

Afferent arrives at the CNS.

Efferent exits the CNS.

Interneurons integrate.

Sensory Afferent; Motor Efferent

SAME pairs pathway role with directional term.

A motor neuron is also called efferent; the first neuron from a receptor is sensory/afferent, not motor.

Understanding sensory signals can improve communication about appetite, pain or function without turning a report into a diagnosis.

Receptor: Detects change

Afferent neuron: Toward CNS

Interneuron: Integrates

Efferent neuron: Away from CNS

Effector: Responds
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Neuron shapes and parts
knowledge.text:
Dendrites receive, the soma maintains, and the axon conducts away.

A neuron has a cell body, dendrites and usually one axon. Multipolar neurons have many dendrites and one axon and are common among motor neurons and interneurons. Most general sensory neurons are unipolar; bipolar neurons occur in special sensory pathways.

Neuron shape and pathway role are related but not identical labels. A neuron may be called sensory because of information direction and unipolar because of structure.

Dendrites receive input.

The axon carries signals away from the soma.

Multipolar neurons have many dendrites.

Most general sensory neurons are unipolar.

Bipolar neurons serve special senses.

Multipolar · Unipolar · Bipolar

Picture many, one, and two processes.

The soma is metabolically essential; a long axon depends on transport from its cell body.

Neural anatomy can explain why sensory and motor effects differ, but symptom localization belongs to trained clinicians.

Multipolar: Many dendrites, one axon

Unipolar: Single process; common sensory form

Bipolar: Two processes; special senses

knowledge.title: Neuroglia are active partners
knowledge.text:
Different glia support, defend, insulate and circulate fluid.

Astrocytes form a supporting network and help regulate the CNS environment. Oligodendrocytes form myelin in the CNS; Schwann cells form myelin in the PNS. Microglia are phagocytic defenders, and ependymal cells line fluid-filled CNS spaces.

Satellite cells support neuron cell bodies in peripheral ganglia. Glia are more numerous than neurons in many regions; the claim that more than 60% of all brain cells are neurons is therefore not a safe generalization.

Astrocytes support and regulate.

Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons.

Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons.

Microglia defend.

Ependymal cells line ventricles/central canal.

Oligodendrocyte in the CNS; Schwann in the PNS

Anchor the myelin cells by location.

A single oligodendrocyte can myelinate parts of several CNS axons; one Schwann cell wraps one PNS segment.

Adequate overall nutrition supports nervous-system health, but no food can be inferred to repair a specific myelin disorder.

Oligodendrocyte: CNS myelin

Schwann cell: PNS myelin

Microglia: Defense

Ependymal: Fluid-space lining

knowledge.title: Action potentials and synapses
knowledge.text:
Electrical conduction along an axon becomes chemical signaling at many synapses.

At rest, ion gradients create a membrane potential. A sufficient stimulus opens voltage-gated channels: sodium entry depolarizes the membrane, then potassium movement helps repolarize it. The refractory period supports one-way propagation from the trigger zone along the axon.

Myelin speeds conduction because current effectively jumps between nodes. At a chemical synapse, the action potential triggers neurotransmitter release; transmitter crosses the cleft, binds receptors and changes the next cell. Acetylcholine is a common transmitter, but the body uses many others.

Sodium entry drives depolarization.

Potassium movement supports repolarization.

Myelin increases conduction speed.

Neurotransmitters cross chemical synapses.

Refractory behavior supports one-way travel.

Sodium depolarizes; potassium helps restore

Then transmitter carries the message across the gap.

Unmyelinated fibers conduct along the full membrane and are generally slower than comparable myelinated fibers.

Claims about stimulants, depressants or supplements require dose and context; anatomy alone cannot predict individual effects.

Depolarize: Na⁺ entry

Repolarize: K⁺ shift

Conduct: Along axon

Transmit: Neurotransmitter across cleft

knowledge.title: Gray, white, tract, nerve, nucleus, ganglion
knowledge.text:
The same cellular material receives different names by location.

Gray matter contains many neuron cell bodies, dendrites and synapses; white matter contains many myelinated axons. In the spinal cord, gray matter forms an inner butterfly-like region surrounded by white columns.

A bundle of axons inside the CNS is a tract; outside it is a nerve. A cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS is a nucleus; outside it is a ganglion. These paired terms are frequent test targets.

Gray matter emphasizes somas and dendrites.

White matter emphasizes myelinated axons.

CNS axon bundle = tract.

PNS axon bundle = nerve.

PNS cell-body cluster = ganglion.

Tract/Nucleus in CNS; Nerve/Ganglion in PNS

Ganglion and ganglia refer to the same PNS cell-body structure in singular and plural.

Clear pathway language helps explain why spinal and peripheral problems can produce different patterns without diagnosing the site.

PNS bundle: Nerve

CNS somas: Nucleus

PNS somas: Ganglion

knowledge.title: Cord, roots and mixed spinal nerves
knowledge.text:
Sensory and motor fibers separate at roots but combine in each spinal nerve.

The spinal cord continues from the medulla oblongata through the vertebral canal. Dorsal roots bring sensory information into the cord, and their dorsal-root ganglia contain sensory neuron cell bodies. Ventral roots carry motor output away.

A dorsal and ventral root unite to form a mixed spinal nerve, so every spinal nerve carries both sensory and motor fibers. The epidural space lies between the vertebral canal and the dura mater and contains cushioning tissue and vessels.

Cord continues from medulla oblongata.

Dorsal root is sensory.

Ventral root is motor.

All spinal nerves are mixed.

Epidural space lies outside the dura.

Dorsal Afferent; Ventral Efferent

Then the roots unite into a mixed nerve.

The adult spinal cord ends above the lowest vertebrae; lower roots descend before exiting.

Spinal pathway knowledge supports safe interdisciplinary communication when function, swallowing or mobility is affected.

Dorsal-root ganglion: Sensory somas

Ventral root: Motor output

Spinal nerve: Mixed fibers

Epidural space: Outside dura

knowledge.title: The reflex arc
knowledge.text:
A reflex can produce a rapid response before conscious interpretation.

A basic somatic reflex arc includes receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron and skeletal-muscle effector. Some reflexes are monosynaptic; many use interneurons and multiple synapses.

The brain can become aware of the event and modify later behavior, but the spinal circuitry does not need to wait for a conscious decision. Reflex testing therefore samples both sensory and motor pathway integrity.

Receptor detects the stimulus.

Afferent neuron enters the CNS.

Integration occurs in CNS gray matter.

Efferent neuron activates an effector.

Receptor · Afferent · Integration · Motor · Effector

Trace the five stations in order.

A withdrawal reflex and the conscious perception of pain are related but not identical events.

Reflex physiology is not a basis for recommending treatment; unexpected neurologic signs warrant appropriate assessment.

knowledge.title: ANS bridge for this quiz bank
knowledge.text:
Sympathetic mobilizes; parasympathetic supports routine restorative functions.

The autonomic nervous system is the involuntary motor branch serving smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands. Its sympathetic division generally mobilizes the body during challenge, increasing selected activities needed for action; its parasympathetic division predominates during many routine conditions and supports digestion, urination and defecation.

In the textbook framing, acetylcholine is released at parasympathetic nerve endings at target organs, while sympathetic end organs commonly receive norepinephrine. Both divisions use acetylcholine at their first ganglionic synapse. Lesson 11 expands this preview; it appears here because the supplied Lesson 10 quiz tests it directly.

ANS is involuntary motor output.

Sympathetic prepares for challenge.

Parasympathetic supports rest-and-digest functions.

ACh is used at parasympathetic target endings.

Both divisions use ACh before the ganglion.

Sympathetic mobilizes, parasympathetic maintains

Use the pattern, not the idea that one division is always on alone.

The two divisions often have opposing effects, yet both continuously contribute to organ regulation.

Digestive symptoms are not proof of a particular autonomic disorder; anatomy helps frame questions, not self-diagnose.

Parasympathetic: Restore and maintain

Shared first synapse: ACh

Parasympathetic target: ACh

Common sympathetic target: Norepinephrine

knowledge.title: Cerebrum and lobes
knowledge.text:
The cerebral cortex supports conscious sensation, movement and higher processing.

The longitudinal fissure separates right and left cerebral hemispheres, while the corpus callosum connects them. Gyri are raised folds and sulci are shallower grooves; folding expands cortical surface area.

The frontal lobe supports planning and voluntary motor control; parietal regions process somatic sensation; temporal regions contribute to hearing and memory; the occipital lobe receives and interprets visual input. These functions operate through networks rather than isolated boxes.

Longitudinal fissure separates hemispheres.

Corpus callosum connects hemispheres.

Gyri are folds.

Occipital lobe is the visual anchor.

Cortical functions are networked.

Front · Parietal · Temporal · Occipital

Move front-to-back around the cortex.

The cerebral hemispheres are highly interconnected; “left brain/right brain personality” claims are oversimplified.

Neurologic changes can affect eating behavior or food skills, but nutrition assessment should not infer a lesion location.

Parietal: Body sensation

Temporal: Hear and remember

Occipital: See

knowledge.title: Diencephalon, brainstem and cerebellum
knowledge.text:
Relay, homeostasis, vital pathways and movement coordination occupy different regions.

The thalamus relays much sensory information toward the cortex. The hypothalamus links neural and endocrine regulation and helps govern temperature, appetite, thirst and autonomic activity; the infundibulum connects it to the pituitary. The pineal gland secretes melatonin.

Midbrain, pons and medulla form the brainstem; ascending and descending tracts pass through it, and the medulla continues as the spinal cord. The reticular formation supports arousal. The cerebellum coordinates timing, balance and complex skeletal movement rather than intellectual processes or emotions.

Thalamus is a major relay.

Hypothalamus regulates homeostasis and pituitary control.

Infundibulum connects hypothalamus and pituitary.

Reticular formation supports arousal.

Cerebellum coordinates movement.

Thalamus · Hypothalamus · Reticular · Cerebellum

Attach relay, homeostasis, arousal and coordination.

The medulla contains pathways linking spinal cord and higher brain regions as well as important autonomic centers.

Appetite and thirst have hypothalamic components but are also shaped by environment, learning, hormones and health.

Thalamus: Relay

Hypothalamus: Homeostasis

Brainstem: Pathways/vital centers

Reticular formation: Arousal

Cerebellum: Coordination

knowledge.title: Meninges, CSF and circulation
knowledge.text:
Three membranes and circulating fluid cushion vulnerable neural tissue.

From outside inward, the meninges are dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulates through ventricles and the subarachnoid space, providing buoyancy, cushioning and chemical stability.

The brain requires continuous blood flow. An interrupted vessel can produce a cerebrovascular accident, or stroke; an aneurysm is a dilation of a vessel wall that may rupture. These are urgent medical concerns, not conditions to assess through nutrition symptoms alone.

Dura is outermost.

Arachnoid is middle.

Pia closely follows brain surface.

CSF cushions CNS.

Stroke and aneurysm are vascular terms.

Dura · Arachnoid · Pia

Recall meninges from outer to inner.

Meningitis affects meninges; encephalitis affects brain tissue itself.

Swallowing or cognition changes after a neurologic event call for coordinated clinical and nutrition care.

Arachnoid: Web-like middle

Subarachnoid space: CSF

Pia: Delicate inner

knowledge.title: Cranial-nerve anchors
knowledge.text:
Learn tested functions before attempting all details at once.

Twelve pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain. The trigeminal nerve is the largest and carries facial sensation plus chewing motor fibers. The hypoglossal nerve controls tongue movements; the vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance information.

The abducens nerve is motor and moves the eyeball laterally. The optic nerve carries visual information and exits the eye at the optic disc. Cranial nerves may be sensory, motor or mixed.

Trigeminal is the largest cranial nerve.

Hypoglossal moves tongue.

Vestibulocochlear serves hearing/balance.

Abducens moves the eye.

Optic carries vision.

Trigeminal · Abducens · Vestibulocochlear · Optic · Hypoglossal

Use the tested anchors, then add the remaining nerves later.

The lacrimal gland makes tears; it is a gland, not a cranial nerve.

Tongue, chewing, smell and swallowing functions can affect intake; refer new deficits and collaborate on safe strategies.

VI Abducens: Eye movement

VIII Vestibulocochlear: Hearing/balance

knowledge.title: Somatic versus autonomic motor output
knowledge.text:
The effector identifies the motor branch.

Somatic motor pathways control skeletal muscle. Autonomic pathways regulate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands through a two-neuron chain with a peripheral ganglion.

Sympathetic output generally prepares the body for challenge; parasympathetic output supports routine, nonstressful functions such as digestion. Both divisions usually maintain some activity, so “fight or flight” and “rest and digest” are useful anchors rather than complete descriptions.

Somatic targets skeletal muscle.

Autonomic targets smooth/cardiac muscle and glands.

ANS uses a two-neuron chain.

Sympathetic mobilizes.

Parasympathetic maintains/restores.

Somatic starts with S, as does skeletal

Autonomic covers organs and glands.

The somatic system does not regulate internal organs; that function belongs mainly to autonomic motor pathways.

Stress can affect appetite and digestion, but an autonomic diagnosis cannot be made from dietary patterns.

Somatic: Skeletal muscle

Sympathetic: Mobilizing ANS

Parasympathetic: Restorative ANS

knowledge.title: Transmitters and organ effects
knowledge.text:
Ganglionic and target synapses use different transmitter patterns.

Both autonomic divisions release acetylcholine from preganglionic neurons. Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons also typically release acetylcholine; most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine.

Effects depend on receptor type and target organ. Sympathetic activity can increase cardiac output and redirect resources, while parasympathetic activity can promote digestive motility and secretion. The divisions are coordinated, not moral opposites.

All preganglionic ANS neurons use ACh.

Parasympathetic target endings use ACh.

Most sympathetic target endings use norepinephrine.

Effect depends on receptor and organ.

ACh first; ACh parasympathetic, NE sympathetic at targets

Track each synapse separately.

Exceptions exist, so transmitter patterns should be learned as common organization rather than absolute rules.

Discuss stress-support habits without implying that one meal can “switch off” sympathetic activity.

knowledge.title: Layers and the light path
knowledge.text:
The cornea and lens focus; the retina transduces.

The sclera is the tough outer coat; its transparent anterior portion is the cornea. The vascular middle layer includes choroid, ciliary body and iris. The iris controls pupil diameter and therefore light entry. The retina is the inner photosensitive layer.

Light passes through cornea, aqueous humor, pupil, lens and vitreous humor before reaching the retina. The lens changes shape for near or far focus. Neural signals leave at the optic disc, a region without photoreceptors.

Cornea is transparent outer layer.

Iris regulates pupil diameter.

Lens focuses light.

Retina contains photoreceptors.

Optic disc is the nerve exit.

Cornea · Pupil · Lens · Retina · Optic nerve

A simplified route to reconstruct under test pressure.

The fovea centralis is specialized for high-acuity vision, whereas the optic disc creates a blind spot.

Vision changes can alter shopping and food preparation; adapt materials while referring new visual symptoms.

knowledge.title: Rods and cones
knowledge.text:
Sensitivity and color discrimination trade off.

Rods are highly sensitive and support dim-light, noncolor vision. Cones require more light and support color vision and fine detail; they are densely concentrated in the fovea.

Photoreceptors pass signals through retinal circuits to ganglion-cell axons, which form the optic nerve. The brain then interprets the patterned activity; the eye does not produce a finished picture on its own.

Rods work well in dim light.

Rods do not provide color vision.

Cones support color and detail.

Cones need brighter light.

Optic nerve is formed by ganglion-cell axons.

Nutrition assessment can evaluate intake while ocular evaluation identifies the cause of vision change.

knowledge.title: From sound wave to cochlea
knowledge.text:
Outer ear collects, middle ear transfers, inner ear transduces.

Sound waves enter the auditory canal and vibrate the tympanic membrane. The malleus, incus and stapes transmit the vibration to the oval window, creating fluid waves in the cochlea that bend sensory hair cells.

Signals travel through the cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve. The semicircular ducts detect rotational movements, while vestibular structures respond to linear acceleration and head position.

Ossicles transmit vibration.

Stapes contacts oval window.

Cochlear hair cells transduce sound.

Vestibular apparatus supports balance.

Tympanic membrane · Ossicles · Cochlea

Use the three main stages, then add details.

The auditory tube helps equalize middle-ear pressure; it is not the main sound receptor.

Hearing or balance barriers may affect counselling format and food-safety tasks; accommodate and refer appropriately.

knowledge.title: Keep neurologic terms distinct
knowledge.text:
Tissue, mechanism and clinical course determine the label.

Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges; encephalitis is inflammation of brain tissue. Multiple sclerosis involves progressive demyelination in the CNS. Alzheimer disease produces progressive cognitive deterioration, while Parkinson disease is associated with movement-control circuitry.

A stroke results from interrupted or bleeding cerebral circulation; an aneurysm is an abnormal vessel-wall dilation. Epilepsy involves recurrent seizure tendency. These summaries support vocabulary only—diagnosis requires clinical evaluation.

Meningitis affects meninges.

Encephalitis affects brain tissue.

Multiple sclerosis involves CNS demyelination.

Stroke is a vascular brain event.

Aneurysm is vessel-wall dilation.

Meningitis · Encephalitis · MS · Stroke · Aneurysm

Attach each term to its primary tissue/mechanism.

Similar symptoms can arise from very different processes, which is why pattern-matching is unsafe.

Neurologic conditions may change energy needs, swallowing or self-management; nutrition care should be coordinated with the clinical team.

knowledge.title: Endocrine versus exocrine
knowledge.text:
Ductless endocrine glands release to blood; exocrine glands use ducts.

Endocrine glands secrete hormones into interstitial fluid and then the bloodstream. Hormones circulate throughout the body, but only target cells with suitable receptors respond. Exocrine glands send products through ducts to a surface or lumen.

Neural and endocrine control interact: neural signals are typically rapid and targeted, whereas hormonal signals may begin more slowly and persist longer. The hypothalamus is a central bridge between the systems.

Receptors create target specificity.

Exocrine glands use ducts.

Hypothalamus links nervous and endocrine control.

Endocrine goes inward to circulation; exocrine exits by duct

Use route, not product name alone.

The pancreas has both endocrine islets and exocrine digestive tissue.

Nutrition interacts with endocrine variables, but hormone symptoms require clinical assessment and laboratory context.

knowledge.title: Hormone chemistry and receptors
knowledge.text:
Protein, steroid and modified amino-acid hormones signal differently.

Protein and peptide hormones, including insulin and growth hormone, are water soluble and generally bind membrane receptors, activating internal second-messenger pathways. Steroid hormones, including cortisol and testosterone, are lipid soluble and bind intracellular receptors that influence gene expression.

Modified amino-acid hormones include epinephrine and thyroid hormones. Their behavior depends on structure: catecholamines use membrane receptors, while thyroid hormone acts more like a lipid-soluble signal.

Cortisol and testosterone are steroids.

Epinephrine is a modified amino acid.

Water-soluble hormones use membrane receptors.

Steroids use intracellular receptors.

Class first, then attach examples.

A hormone’s chemistry helps predict receptor location, not whether it is “stronger.”

Supplements marketed as “hormone balancing” should be evaluated critically; foods do not act as interchangeable replacements for prescribed hormones.

Steroid: Cortisol, testosterone

knowledge.title: Negative feedback
knowledge.text:
The response reduces the original drive and stabilizes a variable.

In negative feedback, rising hormone or target-variable levels inhibit further secretion from upstream sources. For example, hypothalamic TRH stimulates pituitary TSH, which stimulates thyroid hormone; adequate thyroid hormone then reduces TRH and TSH drive.

Positive feedback amplifies a process for a limited event. Oxytocin-driven uterine contractions during childbirth are a classic example: contraction promotes additional oxytocin signaling until birth ends the loop.

Negative feedback opposes change.

Rising end hormone can inhibit upstream signals.

TRH → TSH → thyroid hormone.

Oxytocin can participate in positive feedback.

TRH from hypothalamus triggers pituitary TSH

Then thyroid hormone feeds back.

Feedback is dynamic; a single hormone measurement is interpreted with timing and related signals.

Dietary intake can influence substrates such as iodine, but it does not replace evaluating the entire regulatory axis.

Anterior pituitary: Tropic hormone

Target gland: End hormone

Feedback: End hormone reduces upstream drive

knowledge.title: Anterior and posterior pituitary
knowledge.text:
One lobe synthesizes several hormones; the other stores and releases hypothalamic hormones.

The pituitary, or hypophysis, has two major lobes. The anterior pituitary produces growth hormone, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin and MSH. GH supports growth and metabolism; MSH can increase pigmentation; LH helps trigger ovulation; prolactin supports milk production after birth.

The posterior pituitary stores and releases oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone made in the hypothalamus. Oxytocin supports uterine contractions and milk ejection; ADH promotes water conservation by the kidneys.

Pituitary is also called hypophysis.

Anterior lobe makes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin, MSH.

LH triggers ovulation.

Prolactin supports milk production.

Posterior lobe releases ADH and oxytocin.

Lactation nutrition support should account for physiology and personal goals without interpreting endocrine disorders.

knowledge.title: Thyroid hormones and iodine
knowledge.text:
Thyroid hormone supports metabolic activity; calcitonin participates in calcium regulation.

TSH stimulates the thyroid to produce T3 and T4, hormones that increase metabolic activity in many tissues. Iodine is required to build these hormones. Inadequate iodine can contribute to thyroid enlargement, called goiter, though goiter has more than one possible cause.

Excess thyroid-hormone production is associated with hyperthyroid states such as Graves disease. Severe adult hypothyroid patterns were historically described with myxedema, including fluid accumulation in subcutaneous tissues; diagnosis depends on clinical and laboratory evaluation.

T3/T4 require iodine.

Goiter means enlarged thyroid.

Graves disease is associated with excess thyroid activity.

Myxedema is a severe hypothyroid pattern.

Thyroid hormone requires iodine

Adequacy matters; more is not automatically better.

Excess iodine can also disrupt thyroid function; avoid treating an assumed deficiency without assessment.

A nutrition professional can assess iodine sources and adequacy while medical care evaluates thyroid function.

TSH: Anterior pituitary

knowledge.title: Parathyroid hormone and calcitonin
knowledge.text:
Low blood calcium activates PTH; calcitonin generally opposes that direction.

When blood calcium falls, parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises it by acting on bone and kidneys and by supporting vitamin-D activation, which increases intestinal calcium absorption. The net effect is to defend extracellular calcium needed for nerve and muscle function.

Calcitonin from thyroid C cells tends to lower blood calcium by discouraging bone resorption, although its role in adult moment-to-moment regulation is smaller than PTH’s. Excess PTH can demineralize and deform bone over time.

Parathyroids release PTH.

PTH responds to low blood calcium.

PTH supports renal retention and vitamin-D activation.

Calcitonin tends to lower blood calcium.

Chronic excess PTH can weaken bone.

PTH raises extracellular calcium

Attach the direction before the mechanisms.

Blood calcium is tightly controlled, so a normal blood value does not by itself prove optimal skeletal calcium stores.

Assess calcium and vitamin-D intake without promising that diet alone corrects a parathyroid disorder.

Low Ca²⁺: PTH rises

Kidney: Retain Ca²⁺/activate vitamin D

Intestine: Absorb more with active vitamin D

Bone: PTH can increase release

Calcitonin: Opposing direction

knowledge.title: Adrenal cortex zones
knowledge.text:
Mineral balance, glucose/stress and androgens map from outer to inner cortex.

The adrenal cortex produces steroid hormones. Its outer zona glomerulosa makes mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone, which promote sodium retention and potassium excretion. The middle zona fasciculata makes glucocorticoids such as cortisol, which influence metabolism and stress adaptation.

The inner zona reticularis produces adrenal androgens. Too little adrenal-cortex output is associated with Addison disease; chronic excess, especially cortisol, with Cushing syndrome. These are clinical diagnoses, not conclusions from body shape or fatigue alone.

Cortex makes steroids.

Outer cortex makes mineralocorticoids.

Cortisol is a glucocorticoid.

Inner cortex makes androgens.

Cushing = excess cortex hormones; Addison = deficiency.

Glomerulosa · Fasciculata · Reticularis

Move outer to inner with the three S words.

Cortisol has normal essential functions; “cortisol is bad” is biologically inaccurate.

Sleep, meal regularity and stress-management habits can support wellbeing but are not treatment substitutes for adrenal disease.

Glomerulosa: Salt/mineralocorticoids

Fasciculata: Sugar/glucocorticoids

Reticularis: Sex/androgens

knowledge.title: Adrenal medulla
knowledge.text:
Epinephrine and norepinephrine rapidly support fight-or-flight physiology.

The adrenal medulla is functionally linked to the sympathetic nervous system. Its chromaffin cells release epinephrine and norepinephrine into blood, extending a rapid challenge response throughout the body.

These catecholamines can increase cardiac activity, redirect blood flow and help mobilize fuel. They are modified amino-acid hormones, unlike the steroid hormones produced by the cortex.

Medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine.

These are fight-or-flight hormones.

They are modified amino-acid derivatives.

Medulla is linked to sympathetic output.

Cortex hormones are steroids.

The inner medulla releases rapid challenge signals

Contrast it with the steroid cortex.

A short stress response is adaptive; chronic symptoms have many possible contributors.

Nutrition counselling can address practical eating patterns under stress without claiming to normalize catecholamines.

Cortex: Slower steroid signals

Medulla: Rapid catecholamines

Epinephrine/NE: Fight-or-flight

knowledge.title: Insulin and glucagon
knowledge.text:
Pancreatic islets defend blood glucose in opposite directions.

Beta cells release insulin when blood glucose rises. Insulin supports glucose uptake in responsive tissues and storage, so blood glucose falls. Alpha cells release glucagon when glucose is low; glucagon stimulates the liver to break down glycogen and produce/release glucose.

Diabetes mellitus involves inadequate insulin production, impaired insulin action, or both. Polydipsia means excessive thirst; polyuria is excessive urination; polyphagia is excessive hunger. These signs require assessment rather than self-diagnosis.

Beta cells make insulin.

Alpha cells make glucagon.

Insulin lowers circulating glucose.

Glucagon raises it through liver action.

Polydipsia means excessive thirst.

Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon gives glucose back

Use the directional contrast.

Insulin and glucagon often act together across meals and fasting rather than as isolated switches.

Nutrition care is central in diabetes management but should align with diagnosis, medications and individualized plans.

High glucose: Insulin from beta cells

Storage/uptake: Glucose falls

Low glucose: Glucagon from alpha cells

Liver output: Glucose rises

knowledge.title: Gonads, prolactin and melatonin
knowledge.text:
Reproductive signals and circadian timing complete the endocrine map.

The ovaries produce estrogens and progesterone; testes produce testosterone. FSH and LH from the anterior pituitary regulate gonadal function, with LH triggering ovulation. Testosterone and related anabolic steroids have androgenic and anabolic effects; nonmedical use carries risks.

Prolactin supports milk production after childbirth. The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which helps regulate circadian rhythms. Seasonal changes in light can influence melatonin timing, but seasonal affective disorder is more complex than simply “too much melatonin.”

FSH/LH regulate gonads.

LH triggers ovulation.

Prolactin supports milk production.

Pineal gland makes melatonin.

Melatonin helps set circadian rhythms.

Prolactin · LH · Melatonin

Milk production, ovulation, biological night.

Anabolic steroids are variants related to testosterone; they are not the same category as stimulants or depressants.

Sleep timing can affect eating patterns; address habits and environment without treating sleep or mood disorders outside scope.

Gonads: Sex steroids

FSH/LH: Pituitary control

Prolactin: Milk production

Pineal: Melatonin

Melatonin: Circadian timing

lessons.title: The Blood
lessons.summary: Blood transports materials, stabilizes the internal environment, and limits harm; it is more than a carrier for oxygen.

knowledge.title: Blood is a moving connective tissue
knowledge.text:
Blood transports materials, stabilizes the internal environment, and limits harm; it is more than a carrier for oxygen.

Blood is classified as connective tissue because living cells are suspended in an extracellular matrix called plasma. Its transport work includes respiratory gases, nutrients, hormones, heat, and wastes. Its regulatory work supports temperature, fluid balance, and acid–base conditions, while its protective work includes immune defence and hemostasis.

A useful first distinction is concentration versus total amount. A laboratory value reports what is present in a sample under specific conditions; hydration, timing, illness, altitude, and many other factors may influence interpretation. One result is evidence to place in context, not a stand-alone diagnosis.

Plasma is the liquid matrix.

Formed elements are erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets.

Transport, regulation, and protection overlap.

Concentration and total body amount are not identical.

Transport · Regulate · Protect

Use TRP to recall the three broad functions before naming individual cells.

Plasma volume can change more quickly than red-cell mass, so a concentration can shift even when the total number of cells has not changed by the same proportion.

When discussing a blood result, name the measured marker, the context, and the appropriate follow-up instead of translating one number directly into a nutrition diagnosis.

Transport: Gases, nutrients, hormones, heat, and wastes

Regulate: Temperature, fluid distribution, and pH

Protect: Immune activity and control of blood loss
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Plasma and formed elements tell different parts of the story
knowledge.text:
Plasma carries dissolved materials; formed elements perform cell-based transport, defence, and hemostasis.

Plasma is mostly water, but its proteins and dissolved solutes make it physiologically active. Albumin contributes to fluid distribution, globulins include transport and immune proteins, and fibrinogen is a precursor used in clot formation. Electrolytes, nutrients, gases, hormones, and wastes travel within this medium.

The formed elements include erythrocytes, several leukocyte families, and platelets. A complete blood count separates these populations because a total blood volume cannot show which component has changed. Reading the compartments first prevents the common error of treating every abnormal blood result as the same problem.

Albumin influences oncotic pressure and transport.

Fibrinogen participates in clot formation.

Erythrocytes are the most numerous formed element.

Platelets are cell fragments, not complete cells.

Plasma · Formed elements · Examine separately

Separate the fluid and cellular compartments before interpreting change.

Serum is the fluid remaining after clotting factors used in coagulation have been removed from plasma.

Food intake can influence some transported nutrients, but a plasma measurement still reflects absorption, metabolism, distribution, timing, and health context.

Plasma: Water, proteins, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, gases, and wastes

Buffy coat: Leukocytes and platelets; a small fraction by volume

Erythrocytes: The dominant cellular fraction
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Hematopoiesis is a regulated production system
knowledge.text:
Blood cells arise from stem-cell lineages in red bone marrow and are produced in response to changing needs.

Hematopoiesis begins with multipotent stem cells in red bone marrow. Through branching lineages, these precursors become erythrocytes, leukocytes, or platelet-producing megakaryocytes. Growth factors and hormones regulate the rate and direction of production rather than all cell types being made equally at all times.

Reduced oxygen delivery stimulates the kidneys to increase erythropoietin signalling, which supports erythrocyte production in marrow. Production also requires raw materials such as amino acids, iron, folate, and vitamin B12. A nutrient is necessary for the pathway, but its necessity does not prove that every low blood count is caused by diet.

Red bone marrow is the main production site.

Stem cells branch into specialized lineages.

Kidney oxygen sensing influences erythropoietin.

Adequate substrates do not replace investigation of blood loss, inflammation, or marrow disease.

Marrow · Signal · Mature · Release

Trace a blood cell from origin to circulation.

Erythropoietin is a signal, not an iron source; marrow still needs appropriate substrates and functional tissue.

A nutrition history can identify possible gaps, but persistent or significant blood abnormalities require clinical evaluation rather than automatic supplementation.

Stem cell: Self-renewing marrow precursor

Lineage signals: Direct development toward red cells, white cells, or platelets

Maturation: Cells acquire their specialized structure and function

Release: Mature elements enter circulation
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Erythrocyte shape supports gas transport
knowledge.text:
A biconcave, flexible, nucleus-free erythrocyte devotes space to hemoglobin and moves through tiny capillaries.

Mature erythrocytes are flexible biconcave discs. The shape increases surface area relative to volume and shortens diffusion distance. Loss of the nucleus and most organelles creates room for hemoglobin, but it also limits repair and protein synthesis, so erythrocytes have a finite life span.

Hemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly and participates in carbon-dioxide and acid–base transport. Old or damaged erythrocytes are removed mainly by macrophages in the spleen and liver; useful components such as iron can be recycled, while heme is processed into pigments excreted through bile.

Biconcave shape improves exchange area.

Flexibility supports capillary passage.

Hemoglobin carries oxygen reversibly.

Iron can be recycled after erythrocyte breakdown.

Surface · Hemoglobin · Adaptable · Passage · Exchange

SHAPE links erythrocyte anatomy to oxygen delivery.

Hemoglobin concentration, erythrocyte number, and hematocrit are related measurements but are not interchangeable.

Iron-rich food may support intake, but fatigue or a low hemoglobin value should not be assumed to be iron deficiency without appropriate assessment.

Biconcave disc: Large surface area and short diffusion path

Flexible membrane: Deforms through narrow capillaries

No nucleus: More space for hemoglobin but little repair capacity

Hemoglobin: Binds and releases oxygen according to local conditions
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Leukocytes divide defence work
knowledge.text:
Leukocyte families specialize in rapid ingestion, inflammatory signalling, targeted immunity, and cleanup.

Neutrophils are rapid phagocytic responders, especially in many bacterial infections. Eosinophils participate in responses to parasites and allergic inflammation, while basophils release mediators such as histamine. Monocytes enter tissues and can mature into macrophages that ingest debris and coordinate responses.

Lymphocytes include B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells. Their roles differ, but together they support targeted recognition, antibody production, cellular regulation, and destruction of abnormal or infected cells. Counts vary with age and context, so a differential is interpreted as a pattern rather than a ranking of which cell is most important.

Neutrophils are rapid phagocytes.

Eosinophils and basophils contribute to distinct inflammatory patterns.

Monocytes can become tissue macrophages.

Lymphocytes support adaptive and cytotoxic responses.

Neutrophils · Lymphocytes · Monocytes · Eosinophils · Basophils

A familiar order aid; always pair the name with its actual function.

A high or low leukocyte count describes a laboratory pattern; it does not by itself identify the cause.

Nutrition supports immune-cell production and function, but no single food can substitute for evaluation of persistent fever, recurrent infection, or an abnormal differential.

Neutrophil: Rapid phagocytic response

Eosinophil: Parasite defence and allergic inflammation

Basophil: Inflammatory mediator release

Monocyte: Macrophage precursor and cleanup

Lymphocyte: Targeted recognition and immune memory
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Platelets start repair but do not work alone
knowledge.text:
Platelets adhere and aggregate at injury; coagulation then stabilizes the temporary plug with fibrin.

Platelets are fragments released from large marrow cells called megakaryocytes. When a vessel is injured, local signals expose surfaces that promote platelet adhesion. Activated platelets change shape, release chemical signals, and recruit additional platelets to form a temporary plug.

Platelet activity is only one part of hemostasis. Vascular constriction reduces flow, and the coagulation cascade generates fibrin that reinforces the plug. Later, repair and fibrinolysis remodel and remove the clot. The system must respond strongly at injury while remaining restrained in intact vessels.

Platelets derive from megakaryocytes.

Adhesion and aggregation form a temporary plug.

Fibrin stabilizes the plug.

Clot formation and clot removal are both regulated.

Constrict · Plug · Fibrin · Remodel

Use the sequence to avoid collapsing all hemostasis into 'clotting.'

Clotting factors circulate largely as inactive precursors so that coagulation can be amplified locally without continuously clotting the circulation.

Vitamin K participates in synthesis of several clotting factors, but changing vitamin K intake can interact with some medicines; medication-specific advice belongs with the prescribing team.

1 · Constrict: The damaged vessel narrows

2 · Plug: Platelets adhere, activate, and aggregate

3 · Reinforce: Coagulation creates fibrin

4 · Remodel: Repair proceeds and fibrinolysis limits the clot
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: ABO type is an antigen–antibody relationship
knowledge.text:
ABO compatibility depends on antigens on erythrocytes and antibodies in plasma; mismatching can cause agglutination and hemolysis.

In the ABO system, erythrocytes may display A antigen, B antigen, both, or neither. Plasma contains predictable antibodies against the ABO antigen a person lacks. If donor erythrocytes carry an antigen targeted by the recipient's antibodies, cells can agglutinate and be destroyed.

The familiar universal-donor and universal-recipient shortcuts refer to specific components and circumstances, not every transfusion product. Modern transfusion practice uses typing, antibody screening, and crossmatching because ABO is not the only clinically relevant antigen system.

Type A cells carry A antigen.

Type B cells carry B antigen.

Type AB cells carry both; type O cells carry neither A nor B.

Compatibility depends on the component and recipient antibodies.

Name what is on the cell; then name what plasma targets

This two-step logic is safer than memorizing arrows without understanding them.

Plasma compatibility runs in the opposite conceptual direction from red-cell compatibility because the transfused component contains different antibodies and antigens.

A nutrition professional should not advise on transfusion selection; the useful skill is recognizing why compatibility testing is a clinical safety step.

A: A antigen; anti-B antibodies

B: B antigen; anti-A antibodies

AB: A and B antigens; neither anti-A nor anti-B

O: Neither A nor B antigen; both anti-A and anti-B
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Rh status adds another compatibility layer
knowledge.text:
Rh-positive means the D antigen is present; Rh-negative means it is absent, but antibody formation usually follows exposure.

The Rh system includes several antigens, with D being the main antigen used in routine Rh typing. A person who is Rh-negative does not normally have anti-D from birth. Exposure to Rh-positive erythrocytes through transfusion or pregnancy can stimulate antibody formation in some people.

In pregnancy, maternal antibodies formed after sensitization may cross the placenta in a later pregnancy and affect Rh-positive fetal erythrocytes. Prevention and monitoring are medical processes. For study, keep the sequence clear: antigen difference, exposure, sensitization, then possible antibody-mediated effects.

Rh status usually refers to D antigen.

Anti-D is generally acquired after exposure.

Sensitization and disease are not the same event.

ABO and Rh are separate classification systems.

D antigen · Exposure · Sensitize · Respond

Use the order to distinguish status from acquired antibody formation.

An antibody screen provides information beyond the ABO/Rh label because other erythrocyte antigens can also matter.

If a client raises pregnancy or transfusion concerns, explain the basic mechanism without recommending testing or treatment; refer the question to the appropriate clinical team.

Antigen difference: Rh-negative person encounters Rh-positive cells

Exposure: Transfusion or fetomaternal blood contact

Sensitization: Immune system forms anti-D

Later exposure: Antibodies may respond more rapidly
