lessons.title: Toddler and Preschool Nutrition
lessons.summary: After infancy, growth generally slows and appetite may become less predictable. A child can eat enthusiastically one day and little the next. That observation belongs beside growth over time, activity, illness, development and the overall food pattern, not beside a demand that every meal look the same.

knowledge.title: A smaller appetite is not automatically a problem
knowledge.text:
After infancy, growth generally slows and appetite may become less predictable. A child can eat enthusiastically one day and little the next. That observation belongs beside growth over time, activity, illness, development and the overall food pattern, not beside a demand that every meal look the same.

The course uses average growth numbers to teach the difference between stages. Averages are not a monthly target every child must hit. Your counselling task is to notice patterns, listen to the caregiver and distinguish ordinary variation from persistent deterioration. Weight loss, pain, swallowing problems or declining intake need clinical assessment rather than reassurance based only on age.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Offer structure without taking over the child’s appetite
knowledge.text:
Caregivers can organize what food is offered, where eating happens and regular opportunities for meals and snacks. The child can respond to hunger and fullness within those opportunities. Structure is different from pressure: a predictable snack is not the same as grazing constantly, and an invitation is not a command to clear the plate.

Start with a small serving and allow more when wanted. The historical “one tablespoon per year of age” rule is a starting-portion heuristic, not a maximum intake, complete meal prescription or test of whether a child has eaten enough. For a 3-year-old, three tablespoons illustrates a small first offering of a suitable food, not a total daily allowance.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Exposure is an opportunity, not a countdown
knowledge.text:
An unfamiliar food may need many calm encounters. Seeing, smelling, touching and tasting can be different stages of learning. There is no exposure number that guarantees acceptance; age, sensory preferences, previous experience and the way the food is offered all matter.

Use a familiar food alongside a small optional new food, model eating it and keep the setting low-pressure. Repeated refusal is not a reason to punish the child or declare the food permanently impossible. Highly restrictive rules and “forbidden food” messages can increase a food’s special status. Ordinary household structure is not equivalent to shaming, bargaining or using hunger to force compliance.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Calculate BMI, then pause before interpreting
knowledge.text:
BMI divides weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. For the supplied case, 22.7 kg and 1.14 m give 22.7 ÷ (1.14 × 1.14), approximately 17.47 kg/m². The test’s rounded measurements and answer options explain why 17.4 is the closest offered number; it is not a separate biological threshold.

Children are not interpreted using adult BMI cut-offs. Assessment needs age, sex, a specified growth reference, accurate measurements and the growth trajectory. “Five years” without exact age does not permit a precise percentile, and historical labels differ from current ones. A calculated value alone is not a diagnosis or permission to put a child on a restrictive diet.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Turn a fat percentage into grams
knowledge.text:
The fat AMDR is 30–40% of energy for ages 1–3 and 25–35% for ages 4–18. Fat contributes energy, essential fatty acids and support for absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Young children should not automatically be placed on an adult low-fat eating pattern.

To convert a percentage into grams, multiply total energy by the decimal fraction and divide the resulting fat calories by 9 kcal/g. A classroom total such as 1,200 kcal is an arithmetic assumption, not a universal prescription for every child. A balanced pattern includes suitable sources such as oils, avocado and age-appropriate nut or seed preparations, while accounting for allergies and swallowing safety.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Keep a fibre shortcut separate from the DRI
knowledge.text:
The older “age plus five grams” shortcut gives 10 g for a 5-year-old. Health Canada’s total-fibre Adequate Intake is 19 g/day for ages 1–3 and 25 g/day for ages 4–8. These are different reference systems, not interchangeable answers to an unspecified question.

The source test’s wording does not identify its framework, and both 10 g and 25 g appear among its choices. Learn the distinction rather than memorizing an unsupported official key. In practice, build fibre through varied foods and adequate fluids; avoid abruptly adding large amounts of bran or supplements that crowd out energy or worsen symptoms. Persistent constipation needs assessment, not simply an ever-higher fibre target.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: A nutrient reference is not a supplement prescription
knowledge.text:
Iron supports oxygen transport and development. The iron RDA is 7 mg/day for ages 1–3 and 10 mg/day for ages 4–8. These are total-intake references; treatment doses for diagnosed deficiency are a different matter. Consider what the child actually eats, including iron-rich foods and reliable fortified products.

Iron and vitamin D deserve deliberate attention, but the source test’s population generalization cannot establish which nutrients a particular child lacks. Review milk and drink volumes, supplements, restricted foods and growth history. A family may need practical food ideas, a label review or a referral. Do not diagnose iron deficiency from tiredness or recommend medicinal iron just because a child has a small food repertoire.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Plan a plant-based pattern, not just a protein total
knowledge.text:
A vegetarian or vegan eating pattern needs deliberate planning for a young child’s small appetite and growth. Review energy density, iron, vitamin B12, calcium, vitamin D and other nutrients alongside protein. A dairy-free label alone does not establish deficiency, and a protein total alone does not establish adequacy.

HealthLink BC advises reliable B12 sources and individualized advice when intake is uncertain. Some bulky, high-fibre foods can fill a small stomach before enough energy is eaten. Nut butters must be prepared safely, and drinks differ greatly in energy, protein and fortification. Plant beverages are not suitable main milk replacements under age two without individualized guidance; a paediatric dietitian can help when a milk-free pattern or multiple restrictions makes adequacy difficult.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Add the drinks before changing the menu
knowledge.text:
The supplied 3-year-old case lists juice at breakfast, lunch, snack and dinner: 8 + 8 + 12 + 12 fluid ounces. That totals 40 fluid ounces, approximately 1.18 litres if US fluid ounces are intended. Fortification does not remove the volume, sugar exposure or potential displacement of other foods.

An incomplete food record cannot diagnose a feeding disorder, but this pattern deserves questions. Confirm the usual amount, cup size, whether the day was typical, other drinks, appetite and stools. A caregiver may be relying on juice because they believe the fortification protects the child. Start by understanding that intention; then explain why a beverage cannot replace a varied food pattern.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Build from an accepted food without hiding the concern
knowledge.text:
The case includes oatmeal, banana, buttered macaroni, crackers and white bread. The concerns are restricted variety and a very large juice volume, not the fact that foods taste bland. Sensory preferences are information that can help design a manageable next step.

Keep an accepted food available while exploring a small, safe variation. For example, a child who accepts macaroni may be willing to explore a sauce separately before it is mixed in. Milk, cheese, a soft alternative or a spread must fit allergy history, nutrition needs and chewing ability. More fortified juice or a juice smoothie is not automatically the solution to a record already dominated by juice. Avoid removing every reliable food at once.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Nutrients do not cancel choking risk
knowledge.text:
A food may contain useful nutrients but still be unsafe in its current form. Young children need a seated, supervised eating setting and foods prepared for their actual chewing and swallowing skills. Whole nuts, popcorn, hard round foods and thick spoonfuls of nut butter are important hazards.

Change shape and texture deliberately: thinly spread smooth nut butter, prepare grapes in small lengthwise pieces, and soften or grate hard produce as appropriate. Never assume a generic food-list answer is safe for every child. Known swallowing difficulty requires an individualized feeding plan; do not independently thicken liquids or change prescribed textures. Caregiver first-aid training complements, but does not replace, prevention.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Know when “picky” is not enough of an explanation
knowledge.text:
Food selectivity exists on a spectrum. A narrow repertoire can reflect sensory preferences, pain, constipation, oral-motor difficulty, anxiety or a combination. Investigate without labelling the child as manipulative. Persistent loss of foods, nutritional compromise or distress can require a multidisciplinary feeding assessment.

Ask about coughing, choking, wet or altered voice during meals, long exhausting feeds, vomiting, pain and growth concerns. A nutrition counsellor can document observations, support feasible routines and coordinate a referral; they do not diagnose aspiration or a feeding disorder from a checklist. Acute inability to breathe, severe allergic symptoms or a child who is seriously unwell requires emergency care, not a routine food experiment.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Do not let a diagnosis become an energy formula
knowledge.text:
Children with cerebral palsy or Down syndrome may have feeding, growth and health needs that differ from those of peers. Mobility is one influence on energy expenditure, but muscle tone, movement effort, body composition, growth and medical status also matter. A wheelchair does not tell you the exact amount a child should eat.

The source test compares a nonambulatory and ambulatory child with cerebral palsy as a broad teaching example. Real care must individualize and monitor. Both too little and too much energy relative to needs can cause problems. Review swallowing safety, meal duration, constipation, medication effects and the care team’s plan. Diagnosis-specific growth assessment is a clinical task, not a reason to aim every child at the same weight.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Describe sensory needs, not stereotypes
knowledge.text:
Autistic children are individuals. Some have strong preferences for texture, brand, temperature, presentation or routine; others do not. Refusal and distress should prompt questions about communication, sensory experience, pain and skills. A general claim that autistic children prefer solids or liquids is not a safe clinical rule.

The test appears to use “Rem syndrome” where Rett syndrome is intended. Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition commonly associated with a change in MECP2 on the X chromosome; feeding difficulties can be part of its care needs. That recognition fact does not permit diagnosis from food choices. Keep genetic conditions, autism and cerebral palsy distinct while recognizing that coordinated feeding support may help across them.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Protect the diagnostic pathway before removing gluten
knowledge.text:
Celiac disease is an immune-mediated condition triggered by gluten, not simply a preference for avoiding wheat. Confirmed disease requires avoidance of wheat, barley and rye, attention to cross-contact and appropriate follow-up. Naturally gluten-free foods can contribute variety, but labels and preparation still matter.

Starting a gluten-free diet before evaluation can make diagnostic testing less reliable. A child with symptoms suggesting celiac disease needs medical assessment rather than an experimental broad restriction directed by a trainee. After diagnosis, a paediatric dietitian can support adequate energy, fibre and micronutrients as well as practical gluten-free food choices. Symptoms alone cannot distinguish celiac disease from other causes.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Transfusion-related iron is not a food-ranking exercise
knowledge.text:
Sickle-cell disease and iron-deficiency anemia are different conditions. Repeated transfusions can lead to iron overload, which is assessed and treated by the hematology team. Do not infer iron deficiency from the word anemia or recommend iron supplements without the treating team’s direction.

The test’s single-food question oversimplifies this issue. It is not a sound basis for banning all iron-containing foods or deciding that low-nutrient snack foods are preferable to balanced meals. Review the written care plan, actual laboratory assessment and clinician advice. Food counselling can support adequate nutrition and practical routines without replacing transfusion monitoring or chelation treatment.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Separate allergy emergencies from routine asthma counselling
knowledge.text:
An allergic reaction to food can include breathing difficulty or wheeze, sometimes as part of anaphylaxis. Asthma and food allergy can coexist, but that does not mean all childhood asthma is caused by food or that removing common foods is a general asthma treatment.

When breathing symptoms begin suddenly after food, the priority is the child’s emergency plan and urgent care, not a trial of another food or waiting for a nutrition appointment. For a known allergy, support the prescribed avoidance and emergency plan and coordinate with the clinician. Do not advise a broad elimination diet solely because a child has asthma; unnecessary restrictions can create nutritional and practical burdens.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Turn the whole story into one feasible next step
knowledge.text:
A food record is a starting point, not a verdict. Ask about several usual days, food access, culture, routines, accepted foods, drinks, supplements and symptoms. The same short list can mean different things when a family is managing sensory needs, food insecurity, a recent illness or an established clinical plan.

Choose an action that addresses the most important concern without overwhelming the family. For a well child, that may be a planned snack with an iron-rich food or a modest change in the drink routine. For a child with growth, pain or swallowing concerns, assessment comes first. Document what you know, what is uncertain, the agreed step and how progress will be reviewed. A useful outcome is safer, more workable feeding, not a perfectly coloured plate.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Map home, childcare and the journey between
knowledge.text:
The whole day may cross home, childcare and transport. Ask who provides breakfast, when lunch and snacks happen, whether containers are manageable and whether something familiar is available. Descriptive information is more useful than calling a child a good or bad eater. Shared routines work best when adults avoid shame and comparison.

Food access changes which suggestions are realistic. Ask privately whether food runs out and whether there is equipment, refrigeration, storage and time. Budget education cannot create income. Respectful support may mean connecting the family with resources or using familiar affordable foods rather than requiring speciality purchases. Keep movement and play separate from earning or compensating for food.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “A smaller appetite is not automatically a problem” in your own words.
recall.answer:
After infancy, growth generally slows and appetite may become less predictable. A child can eat enthusiastically one day and little the next. That observation belongs beside growth over time, activity, illness, development and the overall food pattern, not beside a demand that every meal look the same.

The course uses average growth numbers to teach the difference between stages. Averages are not a monthly target every child must hit. Your counselling task is to notice patterns, listen to the caregiver and distinguish ordinary variation from persistent deterioration. Weight loss, pain, swallowing problems or declining intake need clinical assessment rather than reassurance based only on age.
recall.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “Calculate BMI, then pause before interpreting” in your own words.
recall.answer:
BMI divides weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. For the supplied case, 22.7 kg and 1.14 m give 22.7 ÷ (1.14 × 1.14), approximately 17.47 kg/m². The test’s rounded measurements and answer options explain why 17.4 is the closest offered number; it is not a separate biological threshold.

Children are not interpreted using adult BMI cut-offs. Assessment needs age, sex, a specified growth reference, accurate measurements and the growth trajectory. “Five years” without exact age does not permit a precise percentile, and historical labels differ from current ones. A calculated value alone is not a diagnosis or permission to put a child on a restrictive diet.
recall.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “Keep a fibre shortcut separate from the DRI” in your own words.
recall.answer:
The older “age plus five grams” shortcut gives 10 g for a 5-year-old. Health Canada’s total-fibre Adequate Intake is 19 g/day for ages 1–3 and 25 g/day for ages 4–8. These are different reference systems, not interchangeable answers to an unspecified question.

The source test’s wording does not identify its framework, and both 10 g and 25 g appear among its choices. Learn the distinction rather than memorizing an unsupported official key. In practice, build fibre through varied foods and adequate fluids; avoid abruptly adding large amounts of bran or supplements that crowd out energy or worsen symptoms. Persistent constipation needs assessment, not simply an ever-higher fibre target.
recall.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “Add the drinks before changing the menu” in your own words.
recall.answer:
The supplied 3-year-old case lists juice at breakfast, lunch, snack and dinner: 8 + 8 + 12 + 12 fluid ounces. That totals 40 fluid ounces, approximately 1.18 litres if US fluid ounces are intended. Fortification does not remove the volume, sugar exposure or potential displacement of other foods.

An incomplete food record cannot diagnose a feeding disorder, but this pattern deserves questions. Confirm the usual amount, cup size, whether the day was typical, other drinks, appetite and stools. A caregiver may be relying on juice because they believe the fortification protects the child. Start by understanding that intention; then explain why a beverage cannot replace a varied food pattern.
recall.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “Nutrients do not cancel choking risk” in your own words.
recall.answer:
A food may contain useful nutrients but still be unsafe in its current form. Young children need a seated, supervised eating setting and foods prepared for their actual chewing and swallowing skills. Whole nuts, popcorn, hard round foods and thick spoonfuls of nut butter are important hazards.

Change shape and texture deliberately: thinly spread smooth nut butter, prepare grapes in small lengthwise pieces, and soften or grate hard produce as appropriate. Never assume a generic food-list answer is safe for every child. Known swallowing difficulty requires an individualized feeding plan; do not independently thicken liquids or change prescribed textures. Caregiver first-aid training complements, but does not replace, prevention.
recall.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “Describe sensory needs, not stereotypes” in your own words.
recall.answer:
Autistic children are individuals. Some have strong preferences for texture, brand, temperature, presentation or routine; others do not. Refusal and distress should prompt questions about communication, sensory experience, pain and skills. A general claim that autistic children prefer solids or liquids is not a safe clinical rule.

The test appears to use “Rem syndrome” where Rett syndrome is intended. Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition commonly associated with a change in MECP2 on the X chromosome; feeding difficulties can be part of its care needs. That recognition fact does not permit diagnosis from food choices. Keep genetic conditions, autism and cerebral palsy distinct while recognizing that coordinated feeding support may help across them.
recall.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “Transfusion-related iron is not a food-ranking exercise” in your own words.
recall.answer:
Sickle-cell disease and iron-deficiency anemia are different conditions. Repeated transfusions can lead to iron overload, which is assessed and treated by the hematology team. Do not infer iron deficiency from the word anemia or recommend iron supplements without the treating team’s direction.

The test’s single-food question oversimplifies this issue. It is not a sound basis for banning all iron-containing foods or deciding that low-nutrient snack foods are preferable to balanced meals. Review the written care plan, actual laboratory assessment and clinician advice. Food counselling can support adequate nutrition and practical routines without replacing transfusion monitoring or chelation treatment.

lessons.title: Child and Preadolescent Nutrition
lessons.summary: School-age children increasingly eat where caregivers cannot directly observe them. Lunch periods, clubs, transport, friends and advertising become part of the nutrition environment. Children also develop practical skills: opening packaging, choosing between foods, reading simple labels and helping prepare meals. The counsellor’s question expands from “What is served?” to “Can this child comfortably access and eat it?”

knowledge.title: The lunch that comes home
knowledge.text:
School-age children increasingly eat where caregivers cannot directly observe them. Lunch periods, clubs, transport, friends and advertising become part of the nutrition environment. Children also develop practical skills: opening packaging, choosing between foods, reading simple labels and helping prepare meals. The counsellor’s question expands from “What is served?” to “Can this child comfortably access and eat it?”

Canadian guidance recognizes childhood and adolescence as periods of growth and learning about food. Energy and nutrient adequacy remain central as children approach puberty. The food guide is a pattern to adapt, not a test that each meal must pass.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Read the age band
knowledge.text:
Children reach puberty at different times, so peers of the same age can vary in size and physical maturity. Do not use classmates or siblings as a growth standard. Activity should emphasize participation, skills and enjoyment rather than changing appearance.

Selected Canadian RDAs: ages 4–8: calcium 1,000 mg/day and iron 10 mg/day; ages 9–13: calcium 1,300 mg/day and iron 8 mg/day , for both male and female table categories. These describe total intake, not tablets. Vitamin D’s RDA is 600 IU, or 15 micrograms, daily across these ages.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Time, tools, temperature and trust
knowledge.text:
Involving children in planning and packing lunches can improve practical food skills and help identify foods they will use. School meals can reflect taste, culture and budget.

A useful original checklist is time, tools, temperature and trust . Time: how long is available after lining up? Tools: can the child manage the lid and utensils? Temperature: can perishables stay cold or hot food stay hot? Trust: can the child report an unpleasant experience without being punished for waste?
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Spot the persuasive message
knowledge.text:
Children encounter marketing through characters, games, prizes and digital media. Their developmental stage can make persuasive intent difficult to recognize. Supporting media literacy and reducing exposure are complementary approaches.

Original activity: compare two fictional cereal packages. One has a superhero and “power breakfast” slogan; the other is plain. Ask which information is an advertisement and which is a nutrition fact. Then ask whether either package reveals cost, taste, cultural fit or whether the child can actually access it. The exercise should build curiosity, not teach shame about enjoying a branded product.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Respond without making thinness the goal
knowledge.text:
Preadolescents may start comparing bodies before adults expect it. Respond to comments with curiosity rather than a diet. “What happened that made you think you should eat less?” can uncover teasing, a video or a misunderstood classroom lesson. Do not reassure solely by saying a child is thin; that still makes thinness the condition for being acceptable.

Canadian paediatric advice discourages dieting and appearance-focused commentary, emphasizing supportive conversations and a varied eating pattern. Weight-related bullying and preoccupation with food or body shape deserve attention.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Support activity without a product shortcut
knowledge.text:
For ordinary play and routine activity, water is generally appropriate. Sports drinks and caffeinated energy drinks are different products; energy drinks are not a hydration strategy for children. Longer, vigorous activity and extreme conditions may require an individualized plan.

Original logistics exercise: for an after-school activity, identify where a snack can be stored, when it can be eaten and what meal follows. A sandwich portion and fruit may be more useful than buying a performance product. Ask whether transport costs or equipment fees are competing with the food budget. Do not suggest that food must be reduced on rest days to compensate for less movement.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Support, assessment or urgent help?
knowledge.text:
A counsellor can identify barriers, support food skills and facilitate referral. They should not diagnose nutritional deficiency, interpret growth in isolation or independently treat an eating disorder. Rapid or unexplained weight change, growth faltering, persistent food avoidance and delayed puberty warrant medical assessment regardless of apparent body size.

Ask about pain, swallowing, fatigue, stool concerns, medication effects and distress without assuming one cause. Severe dehydration, fainting with illness or acute breathing problems require urgent clinical attention. A child repeatedly unable to eat should not be left with only a motivational worksheet.

lessons.title: Adolescent Nutrition
lessons.summary: Adolescence combines physical development with increasing independence. A young person may make more food decisions while still depending on adults for groceries, transport, money and permission to use a kitchen. School, employment, sports, relationships and online communities can all shape eating. Good counselling therefore asks what a teenager wants help with and what their day actually permits.

knowledge.title: Start with the teen’s agenda
knowledge.text:
Adolescence combines physical development with increasing independence. A young person may make more food decisions while still depending on adults for groceries, transport, money and permission to use a kitchen. School, employment, sports, relationships and online communities can all shape eating. Good counselling therefore asks what a teenager wants help with and what their day actually permits.

Start with an open invitation: “What would make eating easier for you?” Possible goals include feeling less rushed, having food before practice, learning a low-cost meal or reducing conflict at home. Do not assume the desired goal is weight change. Explain the purpose of questions before asking about sensitive topics.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Enough food before optimization
knowledge.text:
A varied eating pattern needs to provide enough food for development and ordinary living as well as activity. A visually impressive salad is not proof of sufficient energy. Nor does a large body exclude undernutrition. Before discussing supplements or detailed nutrient targets, identify missed meals, long gaps and unavailable food.

Original assessment prompts: What happens between school and work? Is there food after evening practice? Are lunch breaks usable? Does nausea, pain, medication or anxiety interfere with eating? Are foods avoided for taste, culture, ethics, allergy, cost or fear? Distinguish a preference from an inability to access food and from distress that requires clinical review.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Reference value or pill dose?
knowledge.text:
For ages 14–18 , Canadian RDAs include calcium 1,300 mg/day , and iron 11 mg/day in the male table category and 15 mg/day in the female category . These are reference categories, not a complete individualized assessment. Vitamin D’s RDA is 15 micrograms (600 IU) daily .

The reference values describe total usual intake, not doses to add automatically. Clinicians should consider menstrual losses, growth, medical conditions and individual physiology, including the needs of transgender and gender-diverse adolescents, without using table labels to invalidate identity.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Understand the choice before advising
knowledge.text:
A well-planned vegetarian pattern can meet young people’s needs. A vegan pattern requires reliable vitamin B12 sources and attention to energy, protein, iron, calcium and other nutrients. A registered dietitian can help translate the pattern into affordable, usable meals.

Ask what a label means in practice: does “plant-based” describe adding beans, excluding animal foods or eating only a few products? Respect ethical motivations. At the same time, ask neutrally whether foods are increasingly feared or rules are multiplying. Neither dismissing a vegetarian choice nor automatically declaring it nutritionally complete is good assessment.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: The athlete’s missing lunch
knowledge.text:
Distinguish ordinary activity from intensive training. Water generally suits routine activity; sports drinks may have a role in specific prolonged or demanding conditions, but caffeinated energy drinks are different and are not a substitute for hydration or food.

Original planning exercise: place training on the weekly school timetable, then mark meals, snacks, travel and recovery time. Look for practical gaps rather than prescribing a universal athlete menu. A teenager travelling directly from school to practice might need food packed before leaving home and an accessible meal afterward. An athlete with repeated injuries, persistent fatigue or menstrual change needs assessment, not a stronger pre-workout product.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Separate the promise from the pressure
knowledge.text:
Dieting during adolescence can harm physical and psychological health. Weight bias and messages from family, peers, sport and media can shape food restriction. Canadian paediatric guidance supports moving away from weight-focused messaging toward sustainable health behaviours and supportive assessment.

Original conversation practice: when a teen says, “I need to be smaller,” ask what they hope would change. The answer may involve bullying, selection for a team, clothing fit or feeling accepted. Acknowledge the experience without endorsing a restrictive plan. “You deserve to feel comfortable and supported; we can work on the eating difficulties and get help with the pressure” is more useful than debating whether they look thin enough.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Do not wait for a visibly low weight
knowledge.text:
Eating disorders can occur at any body size. Persistent restriction, purging, rapid weight change, medical symptoms or major distress need timely clinical assessment. A generic meal plan is not eating-disorder treatment.

Seek urgent medical help for acute concerns such as fainting, chest pain, confusion, severe dehydration or inability to maintain intake. Do not wait for a visibly low weight. Ask about safety within professional competence and follow local safeguarding procedures. Where serious restriction is suspected, do not prescribe an unsupervised refeeding regimen or interpret laboratory results without qualified care.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

lessons.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

lessons.title: Adult Nutrition
lessons.summary: Energy adequacy and nutrient adequacy are different questions. Energy supplies fuel; nutrients support body functions. An eating pattern can provide enough energy while lacking certain nutrients, or contain nutritious foods while providing insufficient food overall. Canada's dietary guidance explicitly recognizes individual variation in energy needs and cautions that restrictive fad diets may pose nutritional risks.

knowledge.title: Two different adequacy questions
knowledge.text:
Energy adequacy and nutrient adequacy are different questions. Energy supplies fuel; nutrients support body functions. An eating pattern can provide enough energy while lacking certain nutrients, or contain nutritious foods while providing insufficient food overall. Canada's dietary guidance explicitly recognizes individual variation in energy needs and cautions that restrictive fad diets may pose nutritional risks.

In a learning assessment, avoid jumping from a body-size description to a conclusion about intake. A person in any body size may skip meals or have a limited diet. Ask what happens on ordinary workdays and days off. The goal is to understand a pattern, not judge a single photograph or food choice.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Do not make every number a target
knowledge.text:
Dietary Reference Intakes describe requirements for healthy populations by life stage and reference categories. An RDA is intended to cover nearly all healthy people in its group. An AI is used when evidence cannot establish an RDA. The EAR estimates the requirement of half a healthy group; the UL is an upper boundary, not an optimal intake goal.

None of these values diagnoses a person’s deficiency. A total-intake reference is not automatically a supplement dose, and one day below an RDA does not establish deficiency. Consider usual intake and clinical context; specialized needs require qualified assessment.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Keep the meal; adapt the pattern
knowledge.text:
Canada's Food Guide encourages vegetables and fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with plant proteins chosen more often; water is the preferred beverage. It also emphasizes cooking, enjoyment, awareness and eating with others. This is a pattern, not a moral ranking of people or a ban on celebration foods.

The plate illustration uses approximately half vegetables and fruit, one-quarter whole grains and one-quarter protein foods. It depicts proportions, not an individualized portion prescription. A bowl, stew or shared platter can express the same principle. Frozen, canned and dried foods can fit.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Calculate, then state the limit
knowledge.text:
Carbohydrate, protein and fat are all relevant to a varied diet. Canada's reference tables list adult macronutrient distribution ranges rather than requiring a single universal ratio: carbohydrate 45–65%, fat 20–35% and protein 10–35% of energy. The adult protein RDA is 0.8 g/kg/day for healthy adults; it is not a treatment prescription or proof that every person benefits from the same intake.

For study, connect foods to overlapping contributions rather than exclusive boxes. Beans offer protein and fibre; nuts provide fat and protein; yogurt can contribute protein and calcium. “Protein food” does not mean a food contains only protein. Likewise, evaluating fat involves food sources and the broader pattern, not simply avoiding every food with fat.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Ask without diagnosing
knowledge.text:
Vitamin B12: animal-source and fortified foods provide dependable sources. A vegan pattern needs intentional reliable provision. Certain medicines or absorption conditions can complicate status; changing food alone may not address a clinical deficiency.

Vitamin D: Health Canada advises people aged 2–50 to eat vitamin-D-containing foods daily or take 400 IU (10 micrograms) daily. For those 51 and older, it recommends a daily 400 IU supplement as well as vitamin-D-containing foods. This public-health supplement advice is distinct from a total-intake reference value or treatment dose.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Access is not motivation
knowledge.text:
Food insecurity refers to inadequate or uncertain food access because of financial constraints. It is not equivalent to poor cooking knowledge. Canadian research links it with household financial circumstances and adverse health outcomes.

Ask permission before discussing money: “Would it help to consider food cost or access?” Also ask about transport, a refrigerator, a usable kitchen and time. Suggesting bulk purchases to someone without storage can increase waste. Suggesting daily fresh shopping to a shift worker can create another impossible job. With consent, help identify practical community or income-support pathways without promising eligibility or treating emergency food aid as a complete solution.

knowledge.title: Design the shift-work experiment
knowledge.text:
Mina, 34, reports missing lunch, then arriving home extremely hungry. She asks for a strict meal plan but has unpredictable breaks and no microwave. First clarify whether she wants more structure, fewer decisions or help with symptoms. Ask about refrigeration, food access and any medical issues; do not assume her difficulty is discipline.

An original agreed experiment could be assembling a suitable cold meal on two shifts, using foods she already likes and can store safely. A second option is an accessible snack when a full meal break is delayed. Let Mina select the feasible option. Review practicality and satisfaction rather than grading perfection. Persistent dizziness, marked fatigue or unexplained weight changes warrant medical review; meal planning is not a diagnostic test.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “Two different adequacy questions” in your own words.
recall.answer:
Energy adequacy and nutrient adequacy are different questions. Energy supplies fuel; nutrients support body functions. An eating pattern can provide enough energy while lacking certain nutrients, or contain nutritious foods while providing insufficient food overall. Canada's dietary guidance explicitly recognizes individual variation in energy needs and cautions that restrictive fad diets may pose nutritional risks.

In a learning assessment, avoid jumping from a body-size description to a conclusion about intake. A person in any body size may skip meals or have a limited diet. Ask what happens on ordinary workdays and days off. The goal is to understand a pattern, not judge a single photograph or food choice.
recall.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “Do not make every number a target” in your own words.
recall.answer:
Dietary Reference Intakes describe requirements for healthy populations by life stage and reference categories. An RDA is intended to cover nearly all healthy people in its group. An AI is used when evidence cannot establish an RDA. The EAR estimates the requirement of half a healthy group; the UL is an upper boundary, not an optimal intake goal.

None of these values diagnoses a person’s deficiency. A total-intake reference is not automatically a supplement dose, and one day below an RDA does not establish deficiency. Consider usual intake and clinical context; specialized needs require qualified assessment.
recall.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “Keep the meal; adapt the pattern” in your own words.
recall.answer:
Canada's Food Guide encourages vegetables and fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with plant proteins chosen more often; water is the preferred beverage. It also emphasizes cooking, enjoyment, awareness and eating with others. This is a pattern, not a moral ranking of people or a ban on celebration foods.

The plate illustration uses approximately half vegetables and fruit, one-quarter whole grains and one-quarter protein foods. It depicts proportions, not an individualized portion prescription. A bowl, stew or shared platter can express the same principle. Frozen, canned and dried foods can fit.
recall.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

recall.prompt: Explain “Calculate, then state the limit” in your own words.
recall.answer:
Carbohydrate, protein and fat are all relevant to a varied diet. Canada's reference tables list adult macronutrient distribution ranges rather than requiring a single universal ratio: carbohydrate 45–65%, fat 20–35% and protein 10–35% of energy. The adult protein RDA is 0.8 g/kg/day for healthy adults; it is not a treatment prescription or proof that every person benefits from the same intake.

For study, connect foods to overlapping contributions rather than exclusive boxes. Beans offer protein and fibre; nuts provide fat and protein; yogurt can contribute protein and calcium. “Protein food” does not mean a food contains only protein. Likewise, evaluating fat involves food sources and the broader pattern, not simply avoiding every food with fat.

recall.prompt: Explain “Ask without diagnosing” in your own words.
recall.answer:
Vitamin B12: animal-source and fortified foods provide dependable sources. A vegan pattern needs intentional reliable provision. Certain medicines or absorption conditions can complicate status; changing food alone may not address a clinical deficiency.

Vitamin D: Health Canada advises people aged 2–50 to eat vitamin-D-containing foods daily or take 400 IU (10 micrograms) daily. For those 51 and older, it recommends a daily 400 IU supplement as well as vitamin-D-containing foods. This public-health supplement advice is distinct from a total-intake reference value or treatment dose.

lessons.title: Nutrition and Older Adults
lessons.summary: Older adulthood includes people with very different abilities, health conditions, living arrangements and goals. Someone may travel independently at 85 while another person needs substantial support at 65. Ask what matters: preparing breakfast, recovering after hospitalization, enjoying family meals or maintaining enough strength to shop. Nutrition is part of functioning and quality of life, not merely a list of nutrients.

knowledge.title: Find the difficult step
knowledge.text:
Older adulthood includes people with very different abilities, health conditions, living arrangements and goals. Someone may travel independently at 85 while another person needs substantial support at 65. Ask what matters: preparing breakfast, recovering after hospitalization, enjoying family meals or maintaining enough strength to shop. Nutrition is part of functioning and quality of life, not merely a list of nutrients.

Age-related changes can affect appetite, taste, smell, thirst and the practical ability to buy or prepare food. Medicines, reduced income, living alone and changes in the home environment can also influence eating. These factors require individual questions, not assumptions that all older adults are frail or forgetful.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Nutritious is not the same as enough
knowledge.text:
Some older adults need less energy as activity and body composition change, while nutrient requirements remain important. Others need additional support because illness or recovery makes adequate eating difficult. Avoid the blanket instruction to eat less because of age. The practical question is whether the person can obtain enough food and nutrients for their situation.

The National Institute on Aging encourages nutrient-dense variety and protein foods across the day, including options such as legumes, fish, dairy or fortified soy products.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Observe function; do not assign a diagnosis
knowledge.text:
Sarcopenia is a muscle condition, not simply looking thin. The European consensus emphasizes low strength, confirms the condition with reduced muscle quantity or quality, and uses poor physical performance to indicate severity. It can occur before older adulthood. Screening and diagnosis require appropriate assessment; a counsellor should not label someone from age, body size or a single observation.

A useful counselling distinction is body weight versus function . Stable weight does not prove stable muscle function. Ask about changes in carrying groceries or rising from a chair as conversation prompts, not as a substitute for standardized testing. New weakness or deteriorating function deserves clinical evaluation.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: A supplement does not replace assessment
knowledge.text:
Health Canada's public advice for people aged 51 and older is a daily supplement providing 400 IU (10 micrograms) of vitamin D , alongside vitamin-D-containing foods. Do not confuse this supplement recommendation with the total-intake RDA or a clinical deficiency-treatment regimen. Provincial or condition-specific recommendations can differ; review individual advice with the person's clinician or pharmacist.

Calcium-containing foods and adequate overall eating remain relevant; a vitamin-D pill does not replace meals. If someone avoids dairy, investigate suitable fortified alternatives rather than assuming every plant beverage contains equivalent nutrients. Read the label for the actual product.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Hydration within the existing care plan
knowledge.text:
Thirst may become less reliable with age. Regular opportunities to drink can help, and fluids may come from beverages and foods. Québec guidance recommends gradual fibre increases and regular fluids rather than relying entirely on thirst.

This does not justify a universal instruction to drink a fixed large volume. Kidney disease, heart conditions and prescribed fluid restrictions require clinical coordination. Ask what advice the person already follows. Practical barriers also matter: a heavy jug, fear of bathroom access or inability to open a bottle will not disappear after a lecture about hydration.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Chewing is not swallowing safety
knowledge.text:
Dental pain, poorly fitting dentures, dry mouth and swallowing difficulty are different problems. A person who has trouble chewing may tolerate a softer preparation; a person with swallowing impairment needs appropriate assessment. Coughing during meals, wet-sounding voice after swallowing or food seeming stuck are reasons to seek swallowing evaluation, not invitations to improvise thickened fluids.

Do not automatically purée everything because someone is older. Unwanted texture changes may reduce enjoyment and intake, and texture safety is individual. Follow an assessed plan when one exists, and clarify uncertainty with the treating team. Acute choking or breathing difficulty requires emergency assistance, not a routine nutrition appointment.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Nourishment after bereavement
knowledge.text:
Sam, 78, says cooking for one feels pointless and clothes are becoming loose. Do not praise the apparent weight loss. Ask about appetite, access, grief, meal routines and the change over time, and encourage timely clinical review for unintentional loss. Offer support without attempting grief psychotherapy outside your training.

Sam chooses a simple evening meal using familiar ingredients and wants to invite a neighbour once a week. Another person might prefer delivered meals or telephone company; there is no mandatory social solution. Discuss whether an existing family helper can assist, with Sam's consent. At follow-up, ask whether meals were eaten and enjoyed, whether shopping is manageable and whether clinical follow-up occurred. The aim is not merely a completed recipe sheet.

lessons.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

lessons.title: The Counselling Relationship
lessons.summary: A helping relationship is neither a lecture nor an ordinary friendship. It has a purpose, agreed roles and limits. The person seeking help brings knowledge of their life; the helper brings relevant knowledge and skills within their competence. A warm manner is useful, but warmth alone cannot compensate for a plan the person does not want or cannot use.

knowledge.title: Three parts of a working relationship
knowledge.text:
A helping relationship is neither a lecture nor an ordinary friendship. It has a purpose, agreed roles and limits. The person seeking help brings knowledge of their life; the helper brings relevant knowledge and skills within their competence. A warm manner is useful, but warmth alone cannot compensate for a plan the person does not want or cannot use.

Working-alliance literature distinguishes agreement about goals , agreement about tasks , and a relational bond . Research applies these concepts in particular therapeutic settings; it should not be interpreted as proof that a brief nutrition conversation produces the same outcomes as psychotherapy.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Reflect before fixing
knowledge.text:
Empathy means trying to understand another person's perspective and communicating that understanding. It does not require agreement with every belief, sharing the same experience or pretending certainty about feelings. Reflective listening can test an understanding: the person remains free to correct it. SAMHSA describes reflection, open questions, affirmations and summaries as central communication skills in motivational interviewing. Its guidance is written for substance-use treatment; the examples here are educational adaptations, not a treatment protocol.

Avoid making the reflection an accusation: “You are afraid of responsibility.” That claims hidden knowledge and closes the conversation. Keep interpretations tentative, particularly when discussing shame, money, identity or family conflict.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Give each listening skill a job
knowledge.text:
An open question invites a description: “What happens around lunch?” A closed question checks a specific fact: “Do you have a refrigerator at work?” Both can be useful; a rapid sequence of either can feel like an interview conducted for the helper's convenience.

An affirmation identifies a genuine effort or strength: “You found a way to eat during a very unpredictable shift.” Generic praise such as “Good client!” places the helper in the role of judge. A summary selects important themes and checks whether the picture is accurate. These are skills to practise rather than scripts to deliver mechanically.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Offer information without taking over
knowledge.text:
Autonomy means respecting the person's role in deciding what happens in their life. It is not abandonment, indifference or withholding relevant information. Shared decision-making combines clear information with the person's values and preferences; checking understanding can include teach-back. NICE recommends presenting information accessibly and reviewing what matters to the person. This is communication guidance from a UK health-care context, not a statement of Canadian law.

Original advice sequence: ask what the person already knows, request permission to offer information, explain one relevant point, then ask how it fits their situation. “Would a few lunch options be useful?” leaves room for no. If the person declines, clarify whether another concern is more important. Do not turn every conversation into an attempt to obtain the answer you prefer.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Consent has a specific purpose
knowledge.text:
Explain the nature of the service, the helper's actual qualifications, expected activities, costs where relevant, privacy arrangements and limits. Make space for questions, disagreement and withdrawal. CCPA's ethics code emphasizes autonomy, competence, informed consent and confidentiality; it applies to its members and must be considered alongside relevant laws and professional requirements. It is not a universal licence to practise.

In an original nutrition-education scenario, consent to discuss meal routines does not automatically authorize contacting family, recording a session or sharing a food diary. Ask separately when the purpose or audience changes. A signature can document part of a process, but it does not establish that information was understood or participation was voluntary.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Cultural humility changes the plan
knowledge.text:
Cultural humility is ongoing self-reflection about personal and systemic biases; cultural safety concerns respectful engagement and addressing power imbalances, with the experience of the recipient central. These are not achieved by memorizing stereotyped food lists for cultural groups.

Original questions: “Which foods or traditions are important to preserve?” “Who normally decides what is cooked?” “Is there anything about previous health advice that made it hard to trust?” Ask without requiring a person to educate you about an entire community. Do your own learning and welcome correction.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Respond to distress without investigating trauma
knowledge.text:
Trauma-informed approaches emphasize safety, trust, collaboration, empowerment and choice. They do not require a nutrition educator to investigate trauma or provide trauma therapy.

If a discussion becomes distressing, pause, acknowledge the person's experience and ask what would help them feel comfortable continuing or stopping. Do not insist on details to satisfy curiosity. Offer an appropriate referral when needs exceed competence. Immediate danger requires appropriate emergency support, not continuation of an ordinary lesson or meal-planning exercise.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Repair with a changed action
knowledge.text:
Jordan says, “You keep telling me to cook, but I work two jobs.” The helper has offered several recipes without asking about time or equipment. A defensive response would explain why the recipes are healthy. A repair begins with ownership: “I moved to solutions before understanding your day. I'm sorry.”

Ask what Jordan wanted from the appointment. Perhaps the priority is finding a usable meal near work, not learning to cook. Agree on a different task and check whether the change feels more useful. This original case illustrates that repairing a relationship involves changing behaviour, not merely using warmer words. Avoid demanding reassurance that the helper is still a good person.

lessons.title: Behaviour Change Models and Theories
lessons.summary: A theory proposes relationships that help explain behaviour. A model simplifies a process or organizes relevant factors. An approach describes how a practitioner works. These categories overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A memorable acronym does not by itself explain causation or establish that an intervention works.

knowledge.title: Define the change before choosing a model
knowledge.text:
A theory proposes relationships that help explain behaviour. A model simplifies a process or organizes relevant factors. An approach describes how a practitioner works. These categories overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A memorable acronym does not by itself explain causation or establish that an intervention works.

Start by defining the behaviour. “Be healthier” is a broad aspiration; “prepare a lunch before two workdays” identifies an action and context. A health outcome, such as a laboratory result, is not itself a behaviour. Outcomes can change for reasons beyond the action being studied. Ask what the person wants before selecting a model, and remember that choosing not to change is not automatically ignorance.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Readiness is behaviour-specific
knowledge.text:
The Transtheoretical Model, or TTM, includes stages of change together with processes of change, decisional balance and self-efficacy. Commonly taught stages are precontemplation (not intending change soon), contemplation (considering it), preparation (intending and taking preliminary steps), action (recently making the change) and maintenance (sustaining it). Some formulations include termination, where temptation is absent and confidence is high.

Standard stage definitions often use time thresholds; they are operational definitions, not biological boundaries. A person can be maintaining one behaviour and contemplating another. Movement need not be linear; setbacks can involve revisiting earlier work. Stages are not permanent personality types.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Confidence is not the same as benefit
knowledge.text:
Self-efficacy is a belief about one's ability to perform a particular action under particular circumstances. It differs from an outcome expectation: believing that an action would help. Bandura identified mastery experience, observing others, verbal persuasion and interpretations of physiological or emotional states as sources of efficacy information.

Social Cognitive Theory places personal factors, behaviour and the environment in reciprocal interaction. Learning can involve observing models, developing skills and regulating behaviour, not simply hearing facts. Self-efficacy is an important construct within this broader theory, not a synonym for the whole theory. Original contrast: “Taking lunch would help me” is an outcome expectation. “I can assemble lunch even on an early shift” expresses self-efficacy.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Map a barrier before choosing support
knowledge.text:
COM-B organizes influences on behaviour into capability, opportunity and motivation. Capability can be physical or psychological; opportunity can be physical or social; motivation can be reflective or automatic. The components interact, and behaviour can change them in return.

COM-B is central to the Behaviour Change Wheel, which connects behavioural analysis with intervention functions and policy categories. Original application: a person does not prepare lunch. Limited food skills may concern capability; no refrigerator concerns physical opportunity; colleagues discouraging breaks concerns social opportunity; a considered preference for another meal concerns reflective motivation; an established rushed morning routine may involve automatic motivation.

knowledge.title: Listen for ownership, not just enthusiasm
knowledge.text:
Self-Determination Theory, or SDT, distinguishes the quality of motivation, not merely its amount. Its basic psychological needs are autonomy, competence and relatedness. Intrinsic motivation involves doing something for its inherent interest or enjoyment.

Extrinsic motivation involves a separable outcome, but can become more personally endorsed through internalization. Autonomous motivation therefore does not mean that every useful action must be enjoyable. Original comparison: “I pack lunch because my coach will shame me otherwise” expresses pressure. “I pack lunch because it helps me manage my afternoon and save money” expresses personally valued reasons, even if preparing it is not fun.

knowledge.title: Respond to ambivalence without a persuasion trick
knowledge.text:
Motivational interviewing, or MI, is a collaborative, goal-oriented communication approach that pays attention to a person's own language about change. It is particularly concerned with exploring ambivalence and strengthening personally endorsed motivation. Partnership, acceptance, compassion and evocation are central; it is not a trick for making someone agree.

MI can be informed by theories without being identical to TTM, SCT, COM-B or SDT. A stage label does not tell you everything about how to conduct an MI conversation, and using open questions alone does not establish MI proficiency. Training, feedback and attention to the actual interaction matter.

knowledge.title: Turn a framework into a testable next step
knowledge.text:
MAP the specific behaviour, the person's priorities and the likely barriers. TRY one jointly chosen, feasible action linked to a clear hypothesis. LEARN from what happened, including changed circumstances and unintended effects.

This is an original study cue, not a named validated intervention. Describe a fallback before the experiment: “If the early shift changes, what option would still feel realistic?” A lapse is information, not proof of a defective character. Review without demanding a perfect streak. Sometimes the best revision is smaller; sometimes it is environmental; sometimes the person chooses another goal.

recall.prompt: Explain “Define the change before choosing a model” in your own words.
recall.answer:
A theory proposes relationships that help explain behaviour. A model simplifies a process or organizes relevant factors. An approach describes how a practitioner works. These categories overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A memorable acronym does not by itself explain causation or establish that an intervention works.

Start by defining the behaviour. “Be healthier” is a broad aspiration; “prepare a lunch before two workdays” identifies an action and context. A health outcome, such as a laboratory result, is not itself a behaviour. Outcomes can change for reasons beyond the action being studied. Ask what the person wants before selecting a model, and remember that choosing not to change is not automatically ignorance.

recall.prompt: Explain “Readiness is behaviour-specific” in your own words.
recall.answer:

Commonly taught stages are precontemplation (not intending change soon), contemplation (considering it), preparation (intending and taking preliminary steps), action (recently making the change) and maintenance (sustaining it). Some formulations include termination, where temptation is absent and confidence is high.

Standard stage definitions often use time thresholds; they are operational definitions, not biological boundaries. A person can be maintaining one behaviour and contemplating another. Movement need not be linear; setbacks can involve revisiting earlier work. Stages are not permanent personality types.

recall.prompt: Explain “Confidence is not the same as benefit” in your own words.

Self-efficacy is an important construct within this broader theory, not a synonym for the whole theory. lessons.title: Communication Skills
lessons.summary: A technically accurate explanation can still be unhelpful if the client feels judged, cannot understand it, or cannot use it. Effective counselling therefore involves listening for meaning, checking understanding, and agreeing what happens next. The aim is not to win an argument about food.

knowledge.title: Hear the problem before solving it
knowledge.text:
A technically accurate explanation can still be unhelpful if the client feels judged, cannot understand it, or cannot use it. Effective counselling therefore involves listening for meaning, checking understanding, and agreeing what happens next. The aim is not to win an argument about food.

It is to help someone make an informed, workable decision while preserving their autonomy. Consider the difference between “You need to stop skipping lunch” and “What happens around lunchtime on a workday?” The first assumes both the problem and its solution. The second opens space for information: perhaps breaks are unpredictable, food storage is unavailable, nausea makes eating uncomfortable, or the client is deliberately restricting.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Choose a communication tool deliberately
knowledge.text:
OARS stands for open questions, affirmations, reflective listening, and summaries. SAMHSA describes these core motivational interviewing skills within substance-use treatment. Their communication principles can inform nutrition conversations, but this lesson is not training or certification in delivering a complete motivational interviewing intervention.

An open question invites explanation: “What would you like to feel different after our work together?” A closed question obtains a particular detail: “Do you have access to a refrigerator?” Both are useful. Open questions discover the story; focused questions clarify it. Asking only open questions can leave safety details unclear; asking only closed questions can feel like an interrogation.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Follow three possible turns
knowledge.text:
A simple reflection stays near the words: “You feel rushed in the morning.” A more complex reflection tentatively connects meaning: “Having breakfast ready might make mornings feel less chaotic.” More complex does not automatically mean better.

If your interpretation is unsupported, use a tentative phrase or return to a simpler reflection. Compare three responses to “I know what to do, but I never keep it up.” Advice-first: “Set an alarm.” Judgment: “You need discipline.” Reflective: “You have tried before, and you are discouraged that the plans have not lasted.” The reflective response does not solve the problem immediately.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Ask–offer–check, without a hidden agenda
knowledge.text:
Information is often more useful when it answers a question the client actually has. An original teaching sequence is ask–offer–check: ask what they know and whether information would help; offer a small relevant explanation; check what they make of it.

This is a study sequence, not a validated assessment tool. For example: “What have you heard about fibre?” Then: “Would a short explanation help?” After a brief explanation: “How does that fit with foods you enjoy?” Do not treat asking permission as a trick to secure agreement. Someone may decline, ask for another topic, or disagree after hearing the information.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Check your explanation—not the client’s obedience
knowledge.text:
Teach-back asks a person to explain the plan in their own words so you can identify communication gaps. It should be framed as a check on how clearly you explained, not as a memory examination. If understanding is incomplete, explain differently and check again.

An original example: “I covered several things quickly. To check that I explained them clearly, how would you describe the lunch experiment we agreed?” If the person describes a different plan, avoid “No, you weren't listening.” Try “I can see I made that confusing. Let's make the plan simpler.” Teach-back is different from asking “Do you understand?” People may say yes out of politeness or embarrassment.
knowledge.sourceLabel: Existing hub study guide · supplementary learning, not an official textbook or answer key

knowledge.title: Make disagreement useful
knowledge.text:
Shared decision-making connects available options with what matters to the person. Discuss relevant benefits, burdens, uncertainties, and the option of no change where appropriate; agree how the decision will be reviewed. In an original nutrition example, the options might be preparing food at home, assembling convenience foods, or buying lunch. These are not ranked by moral worth.

Compare cost, time, facilities, enjoyment, and reliability. Ask “Which would fit your next week?” rather than “Which is the healthiest choice?” when the latter hides practical trade-offs. If disagreement emerges, slow down. “We may be looking at this differently. What feels unhelpful about my suggestion?”
